boeing.public_statement:
A few years ago we said we had three jobs to do before anything else: stabilize the factories, finish the airplanes we'd started, and repair the balance sheet. The 777X is in service, the MAX 7 and 10 are delivering, and our net debt is back where it was before the hard years. I'm proud of this team for that. We still work on safety and quality every day, and that doesn't stop.

People ask me whether now is the time for the next airplane. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. We're ready on our end. The other two aren't there yet, and I'm not going to launch an airplane to win a news cycle. When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it, and not before.

On the 737 we're holding at 57 a month. The line is stable and the data is good, and the demand in front of us doesn't need another step right now. I'd much rather run a steady line than chase a number. On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep investing in it and in Charleston.

Going slow is what let us go fast. It's so much more important that we do this right than fast.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing in every field.
- fps hold; fps_engine_code null; fps_site new_site (no effect with fps on hold).
- rate_737 hold; re787 hold.
- No order differs from the default, so nothing goes to the Board.
- My record drove the narrowbody calls. On the 787 Re-engine, company doctrine (profile §7's read of the A350 Re-engine odds) drove the call, not my record. My evidence on Airbus is Low.

1. RULINGS ON THE HARD RULES (Board recommendation 2)
- H1 (no fps in Round 1): lifted for 2030. Its 2026 grounds have lapsed:
  - the 777X entered service in 2027 [BX-0550];
  - the MAX 7/10 was certified in 2026 [BX-1299, BX-1873];
  - net debt reached $0.0B in 2029, and 2030 in the stress case (brief §2) [BX-1305, B-2327, B-2326].
  - The condition is met, not waived. An fps still has to win on the grid and pass Malave's buffer test, and this round none does.
- H3, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1): lifted. Its ground was "the 777X comes first" [B-2276], and the 777X is done.
- H3, second half: confirmed. No 787 Re-engine once an A350 Re-engine is on the public record. None is on it today.
- H4: at most 2 years of overlap between a Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine.
  - A 2030 Re-engine with a 2030 10-year fps overlaps 2 years (legal); with a 2030 7-year fps, 5 years (barred).
  - Nothing ordered here engages H4.
- H5, H6 and H8 apply as written. H2 cannot bind. H7 has no trigger.

2. MY FOUR QUESTIONS
(1) Are the KPIs stable? Yes. The brief shows no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Pope's KPI check passes and her veto is not invoked.
(2) Are market, technology and our balance sheet all ready?
- Balance sheet: yes.
- Market: not for an fps. Under this demand case Airbus's unmet demand falls to us, so NGSA alone costs only $0.64B (S2), or $0.83B on the A320 Alt plan (S3).
- Technology: no. At a 2040 EIS every engine code gives CFM only.
- So we are not ready on all three [BX-1296].
(3) What if certification takes longer than we think? Malave ran S6 as the baseline (section 4).
(4) Is this doing less, better? I compared every row against Do Nothing in the same column [BX-1239].

3. THE TESTED CASE AGAINST DO NOTHING AND S6 (Board recommendation 1)
Each row reads S1 / S2 / S3 / S4 / S5 / S6.
- Submitted, Do Nothing: 0.00 / -0.64 / -0.83 / -2.62 / -3.26 / -0.64. S6 equals Do Nothing's own S6.
- There are no Board items, so there are no default rows to show.
- Rejected rows, for the record:
  - B, 787 Re-engine: +3.30 / +2.67 / +2.47 / -5.10 / -5.74 / +2.67. Against Do Nothing: +3.30 / +3.31 / +3.30 / -2.48 / -2.48 / +3.31.
  - C, Rate Increase: -0.21 / -1.20 / -1.66 / -2.83 / -3.83 / -1.20. Against Do Nothing: -0.21 / -0.56 / -0.83 / -0.21 / -0.57 / -0.56.
  - D, best fps (10-year at Renton + Re-engine): -2.19 / -3.24 / -3.90 / -10.59 / -11.64 / -3.26.
  - E, 10-year at Renton: -4.39 / -5.44 / -6.09 / -7.01 / -8.06 / -5.45.
  - F, 7-year at Renton: -7.91 / -8.18 / -8.76 / -10.53 / -10.80 / -8.18.
  - G, best via Embraer row: -21.08 / -22.13 / -22.79 / -29.48 / -30.53 / -22.15.
- Expected column: S2 and S5 at even odds.
  - Do Nothing scores -1.95 on that blend, and the Re-engine -1.535 (+0.41, inside ε).
  - On S2 alone the Re-engine is best (+2.67).

4. MALAVE'S MEMO: binding on the fps, advice on the rest
Buffer test (limit: S6 no lower than -2.64):
- Do Nothing passes at -0.64, $2.00B clear of the limit.
- The Re-engine passes at +2.67, $5.31B clear.
- The Rate Increase passes at -1.20.
- All 24 fps rows fail:
  - D at -3.26, short by $0.62B;
  - E at -5.45, short by $2.81B;
  - F at -8.18, short by $5.54B;
  - G at -22.15, short by $19.51B.
- His veto on any fps launch binds under the team rule. I accept it in full.
"Fundable when the 777X turns":
- 10-year fps: pass. Stress-case net debt is held at $0.0B in all 8 rows.
- 7-year fps: fail. Stress peak $0.7B, $2.8B with the Re-engine, $3.1B in S4/S5. Only the 7-year at Renton without the Re-engine holds.
- Via Embraer: fail. Stress peak $1.0-6.3B.
- Re-engine alone and Rate Increase: pass at $0.0B.
Undiscounted debt penalties, for scale only (the grid already nets them): 10-year $19.1B, 7-year $22.0B, via Embraer $52.5B, Re-engine $0.6B.

5. POPE'S SEAT
- No live problem, so the KPI veto cannot bind.
- The Rate Increase fails capacity-follows-demand.
- The Re-engine passes every operations test:
  - zero overlap;
  - about $1B a year, 7% of base free cash flow;
  - a GEnx derivative meets 2035; Rolls-Royce UltraFan WB arrives in 2036, a year late;
  - Charleston can absorb the volume.
- Her hold on the Re-engine is deference, not a finding.
- She backs the 10-year ramp, and finds that Embraer adds nothing Boeing lacks [BX-1330].

6. THE 787 RE-ENGINE, THE ONE LIVE DECISION
Its value hangs on a sealed Airbus move I cannot see.
- Gain against hold: 3.31 - 5.79p, where p is the odds of an A350 Re-engine this round.
  - Break-even is 57%.
  - The gain falls inside ε at 40% or more.
  - Holding breaks the $2B H8 cap only below 23%.
- Doctrine §7 (an inference; my own record is Low here) expects an early A350 Re-engine attempt: Airbus re-engines cheaply [B-2446].
- At even odds the gain is +0.41, a tie. Doing less [BX-1239], the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] and the higher worst column (-3.26 against -5.74) all break it toward hold.
- The call is robust: at one-in-three odds, holding gives up about $1.38B, still inside the cap. I have no evidence to put the odds under 23%.
- The upside is fragile. The grid assumes nobody moves after this round, and a 2035 A350 Re-engine would stop our gains at 2040 and cut the margin (Malave).
- It fails the Board's -$1B downside limit in S4 and S5 (-2.48), and the Board named hold as the acceptable alternative. A launch I expect to be vetoed is not one well-founded case.
- Doctrine's "Chicken game" inference: sealed same-round orders give no first mover. A same-round match is the -2.48 outcome. Holding keeps the option to stand aside under H3.
- Cost of waiting, which I accept:
  - a 2035 launch is worth about 0.61 times as much;
  - it would overlap a 2035 10-year fps by 2 years ($1.2B strain undiscounted, H4-legal);
  - it rules out pairing with a 2035 7-year fps.

7. RATE INCREASE
- KPIs pass, but the business case fails in every column: -0.21 to -0.83.
- 66, 42 and 20 MAX slots sit idle in 2032-34.
- This is the only round it is offered. Letting it lapse gains $0.56B in S2.
- Not decided with reference to Airbus (H6).

8. fps
- Malave's veto binds, and every row sits below Do Nothing in every column.
- An objective premium of at least $4.39B would exceed the $2B cap.
- I prepare the 2035 case (10-year ramp, Renton, engine code) and announce no date [B-2315, B-2313].

9. PREMIUM LOG
- Doctrine premium: $0.41B (Re-engine hold, even odds).
- Objective premium: $0.
- Total: $0.41B, within the $2B cap.
- It breaks if the odds of an A350 Re-engine fall below 23%.

10. RED LINES
- None is breached:
  - no rate request without stable KPIs;
  - no concurrency of production and certification;
  - no cancel;
  - no fixed-price development;
  - no blame on the FAA;
  - no attribution of a supplier problem to Airbus.
- The overrides list is empty.

rate_737: increase. Its item value is -0.21 / -0.56 / -0.83 / -0.21 / -0.57 / -0.56 alone, -0.94 to -1.28 with a 10-year fps, and -1.06 to -1.30 with a 7-year fps. It is below zero in every column, so the business case fails, and with an fps it also breaches the Downside limit. Under this demand case the MAX at 57 a month already serves Boeing's preference until the 2040s. It is also vetoed if the rationale cites Airbus (H6) or if Pope's KPI check fails. Acceptable alternative: hold.

recommendations.text: Bring us one tested case. Show the full grid row for the plan with Do Nothing and the risk-case column S6 side by side, and the default row for each Board item, and name your expected column. Under this run's assumptions (the conservative demand case, Boeing losing 1 point a year after NGSA enters service, Airbus's unmet demand falling to Boeing, Airbus adding 1% capacity a year), NGSA alone costs Boeing $0.64B (S2) and $0.83B on the A320 Alt plan (S3). The grid does not yet support a defensive launch.

Rule on H1 and H3 in the rationale, with evidence: the 777X entering service in 2027, the MAX 7/10 complete, and net debt at its historical level in 2029 (2030 in the stress case) per brief §2. Lifting them is the CEO's call and we accept a reasoned ruling either way, but our grid tests still govern each item. Also confirm H3's second half: no 787 Re-engine once an A350 Re-engine is on the public record.

Malave's buffer test should be in the package with numbers. Do Nothing is -0.64 in S6, so the limit is -2.64. Every fps row fails it this round, the closest by $0.62B (the 10-year fps at Renton with the Re-engine, -3.26). His 'Fundable when the 777X turns' result should also appear. We read the brief as a pass for a 10-year fps (net debt held in the stress case) and a fail for a 7-year fps (stress peak $0.7B). We do not veto on that leg.

Keep the 787 Re-engine in reserve. It is worth +3.3B if Airbus leaves the A350 alone, but loses $2.48B if Airbus re-engines in the same round, so it fails our downside limit. Show both outcomes in every round you bring it. We will not approve it only because Airbus is quiet, nor reject it on a public statement alone.
Keep 737 rates KPI-gated and agreed with the FAA. The 2032 step ($2.94B) loses value in every column under this demand case. No Rate Increase as a reply to Airbus (H6).

Prepare, but do not announce, the 2035 fps case. Use the 10-year ramp, which has the higher worst column (-8.53 against -11.22 this round). Consider the Renton site, which adds +0.36 to +0.69 in every column. Choose an engine code that names a maker with an engine ready by EIS. CFM alone gives one source in every plan; a second or third source would come only if P&W and Rolls-Royce launch when selected. Engine choice is never a veto ground. Give no fps date before launch, and set a conservative EIS at launch.

Log every premium. An fps launch now would carry an objective premium of at least $4.39B against Do Nothing, above the $2B H8 cap, so the 50/50 share objective cannot justify a launch this round. Once net debt is repaired, what to do with surplus cash is reserved to this Board; no plan should assume it.

frame.question: The 777X and the MAX 7/10 are finished, and net debt is back at its historical level. So in 2030, is Boeing ready for its next development, and which one should it be: the fps, the 787 Re-engine, or neither? And does a 737 Rate Increase, which is only on offer this round, add value? Put plainly: "We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready" [BX-1296]. This round we check all three work streams with data, not dates.

frame.initial_lean:
NARROWBODY: DO NOTHING THIS ROUND.
- fps hold, fps_engine_code null, fps_site left at new_site.
- rate_737 hold.
- Every fps row is below Do Nothing in every column and fails Malave's buffer test; the closest misses by $0.62B. Under this demand case the market and the technology are not ready: NGSA alone costs us $0.64B, and no second engine source is on the record. "Not now on all 3" [BX-1296].
- The Rate Increase loses value in every column, so even with clean KPIs its business case fails. Letting it lapse is a gain, not a loss.
- Holding both gives up nothing, so there is no premium.

WIDEBODY: THE 787 RE-ENGINE IS THE ONE LIVE DECISION, AND I HAVE NOT MADE IT.
- It passes my own tests. H3's first half has lapsed and I am ruling it lifted. It adds $3.3B in S1, S2, S3 and S6. It passes the buffer test by $5.3B and holds net debt in stress. It overlaps nothing, and a 2030 start finishes before a 2035 fps's strain window opens, so it is one development at a time.
- Its value turns on an Airbus move we cannot see: it loses $2.48B in S4 and S5. Break-even odds are 57%, and at 40% odds or more its expected gain falls within ε of hold.
- Company doctrine expects an early A350 Re-engine attempt (§7; Airbus re-engines cheaply [B-2446]).
- The Board has told us it would veto the Re-engine on its -$1B downside rule.

My lean is to hold it in reserve if we judge the A350 risk at roughly even odds; then doing less wins the tie [BX-1239]. If Malave or Pope's seat gives me grounds to put that risk well below 40%, I take it to the Board as one tested case, with all six columns and the S4/S5 loss shown, and accept its veto if it holds the line.

I will not call it a doctrine premium to hold the Re-engine while naming S2 as my expected column. That give-up is $3.31B, above the H8 cap. If it stays on hold, either the odds or the Board's veto will have to carry it.

ALONGSIDE, NOT ANNOUNCED:
- Prepare the 2035 fps case: 10-year ramp, Renton considered, an engine code that could bring a second source by entry into service.
- No fps date before launch [B-2315].
- No date tied to Airbus [B-2313].

"It is so much more important that we do this right than fast" [BX-1241]. "There's no hurry here" [B-2305].

DEFERRAL TO 2035 (inference from the 20-year window and the 10.5% WACC):

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
FOR THE 787 RE-ENGINE:
- A firm public sign that Airbus will leave the A350 alone, such as widebody resources committed elsewhere or a stated no to an A350 Re-engine, would change my advice. If it put the odds below 40%, I would support the Re-engine as one tested case to the Board, with all six columns shown. It passes my buffer test by $5.31B and holds net debt at $0.0B in stress.
- Below 23% odds, holding it breaks the $2B H8 cap.
- An A350 Re-engine already on the public record ends the question under H3.

FOR THE fps: I would change my view on a later brief in which the best fps row sits no more than $2B below Do Nothing in S6 and beats Do Nothing by more than ε in the expected column. NGSA in development, which makes Do Nothing worse, could produce such a brief. In that case I would prefer the 10-year ramp, which has the smaller bill and penalty and keeps stress net debt at $0.0B, at Renton.

FOR THE RATE INCREASE: only a grid showing a positive item value would change my mind, and the move is offered only this round.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran the slip leg as the baseline. Do Nothing scores -0.64 in S6, so the limit is -2.64. Every fps row fails. The closest, the 10-year at Renton with the 787 Re-engine, sits at -3.26, short by $0.62B. The 10-year at Renton alone misses by $2.81B and via Embraer by $19.51B or more. Under the team rule that is a binding veto on any fps launch this round. The 10-year ramp does pass "Fundable when the 777X turns", with stress net debt at $0.0B. The 7-year at a new site or with the Re-engine fails it ($0.7-3.1B), and so does Embraer ($1.0-6.3B).

The Rate Increase passes the buffer but loses $0.21-0.83B in every column. I would not fund it.

The 787 Re-engine passes the buffer by $5.31B and holds net debt at zero in stress, at about $1B a year. My concern is its worst column, -5.74 in S5: $2.48B below Do Nothing's worst, more than my own buffer. Doctrine, not my record, puts an A350 Re-engine at roughly even odds. On that read the Re-engine is worth +0.41, a tie, and the higher-confidence plan wins it. I advise holding, which is not a veto, and logging a $0.41B premium.

That holds barring a firm sign that Airbus leaves the A350 alone. Below 40% odds I would take the Re-engine to the Board; below 23%, holding breaks the $2B cap.

It is a baseline we can meet and potentially beat. We're bullish on our outlook.

ops.would_change_mind_if: (1) KPI veto: a brief reporting a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem would make it binding against any Rate Increase. None is reported. (2) Rate Increase: an item value above zero in the expected column (S2), the idle 2032-34 slots gone, and CFM confirming LEAP-1B supply for +100 a year [BX-1264, B-2308]. (3) 787 Re-engine: operations already passes it, so my hold is deference, not an operations finding. I would back a 2030 launch if Ortberg or Malave put the A350 Re-engine odds well below 40% (expected gain +0.99 at 40%, +1.57 at 30%; about $0.58B per 10 points) and the Board's -$1B rule were met. I would fail it on delivery if the only engine route were Rolls-Royce UltraFan WB (ready in 2036, a year after EIS). (4) fps: a later grid putting the 10-year Solo above Do Nothing by more than $1B in the expected column, within Malave's buffer, with a second engine maker ready by EIS.
ops.memo:
Three results, ranked. My record is Global Services, not Commercial Airplanes: the KPI, strain and supplier gates are doctrine.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery [BX-1331]. Nothing is live. The brief reports no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, so my KPI veto does not bind. The Rate Increase fails on demand, not on KPIs: at 57 a month we already leave 66, 42 and 20 slots idle in 2032-34, and the step loses $0.21-0.83B in every column. Hold it.

Second, engineering capacity: one development at a time [B-0341]. The 787 Re-engine passes every operations test. It has no overlap, costs about $1B a year (7% of base free cash flow), and net debt holds in stress. 2030 is its cleanest window: it finishes before a 2035 10-year fps opens its strain window in 2038. Deferred to 2035, it adds 2 years of overlap to that fps ($1.2B of strain) and rules out a 7-year one. Launching turns on the A350, where I have no record. I defer to Kelly and the Board. We see about $0.58B of expected value for every 10 points of A350 odds; break-even is 57%.

And finally, disciplined profitable growth [BX-1327]. No fps passes today. The 10-year ramp beats the 7-year by $2.65-3.63B in every column; a same-round 7-year fps plus the Re-engine overlaps 5 years (H4). Embraer trails Solo by $18B and adds no IP or capacity we lack [BX-1330]. Prepare the 2035 case on the 10-year ramp.

other_moves.detail: Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line. The KPIs are stable (no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem). The demand in front of us does not call for another step: 66, 42 and 20 MAX slots sit idle in 2032-34. Rates stay agreed with the FAA and gated on data [BX-1259, B-2351].

other_moves.move: Keep growing 787 capacity at Charleston
other_moves.detail: Widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity on today's 787, the most efficient airplane in its segment [BX-1317, B-2336]. The board does not price this.

other_moves.detail: 10-year ramp, which beats the 7-year by $2.65-3.63B in every column. The Renton site is on the table (+0.36 to +0.69 in every column, about $3.0B of capex avoided), alongside Pope's plan for the MAX wind-down: the waiting backlog grows to 792 by 2047 in Do Nothing, so Renton winds down only as fps capacity comes on. The engine code is set at launch. My lean is to keep CFM named (Code 3, an inference), and I will test Codes 5 and 6 against what P&W and Rolls-Royce would need to see to have a second source ready by EIS. Development contracts carry risk-share or cost-plus terms, not fixed price [BX-1262, BX-1304]. No date before launch [B-2315].

other_moves.detail: A low-cost study with GE on a GEnx-derivative route that meets a 5-year EIS; engine durability first [BX-1298]. Rolls-Royce UltraFan WB arrives a year late on a 2030 launch. It comes back to the Board in 2035, with both outcomes shown, if the A350 has not re-engined (H3, second half). Pairing with a 2035 10-year fps gives 2 years of overlap (H4-legal, $1.2B strain undiscounted).

other_moves.detail: Cash for readiness [BX-1243, B-2330]. Supplier readiness stays a hard gate on any future rate step or launch.

decision.public_statement:
A few years ago we said we had three jobs to do before anything else: stabilize the factories, finish the airplanes we'd started, and repair the balance sheet. The 777X is in service, the MAX 7 and 10 are delivering, and our net debt is back where it was before the hard years. I'm proud of this team for that. We still work on safety and quality every day, and that doesn't stop.

People ask me whether now is the time for the next airplane. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. We're ready on our end. The other two aren't there yet, and I'm not going to launch an airplane to win a news cycle. When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it, and not before.

On the 737 we're holding at 57 a month. The line is stable and the data is good, and the demand in front of us doesn't need another step right now. I'd much rather run a steady line than chase a number. On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep investing in it and in Charleston.

Going slow is what let us go fast. It's so much more important that we do this right than fast.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing in every field.
- fps hold; fps_engine_code null; fps_site new_site (no effect with fps on hold).
- rate_737 hold; re787 hold.
- No order differs from the default, so nothing goes to the Board.
- My record drove the narrowbody calls. On the 787 Re-engine, company doctrine (profile §7's read of the A350 Re-engine odds) drove the call, not my record. My evidence on Airbus is Low.

1. RULINGS ON THE HARD RULES (Board recommendation 2)
- H1 (no fps in Round 1): lifted for 2030. Its 2026 grounds have lapsed:
  - the 777X entered service in 2027 [BX-0550];
  - the MAX 7/10 was certified in 2026 [BX-1299, BX-1873];
  - net debt reached $0.0B in 2029, and 2030 in the stress case (brief §2) [BX-1305, B-2327, B-2326].
  - The condition is met, not waived. An fps still has to win on the grid and pass Malave's buffer test, and this round none does.
- H3, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1): lifted. Its ground was "the 777X comes first" [B-2276], and the 777X is done.
- H3, second half: confirmed. No 787 Re-engine once an A350 Re-engine is on the public record. None is on it today.
- H4: at most 2 years of overlap between a Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine.
  - A 2030 Re-engine with a 2030 10-year fps overlaps 2 years (legal); with a 2030 7-year fps, 5 years (barred).
  - Nothing ordered here engages H4.
- H5, H6 and H8 apply as written. H2 cannot bind. H7 has no trigger.

2. MY FOUR QUESTIONS
(1) Are the KPIs stable? Yes. The brief shows no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Pope's KPI check passes and her veto is not invoked.
(2) Are market, technology and our balance sheet all ready?
- Balance sheet: yes.
- Market: not for an fps. Under this demand case Airbus's unmet demand falls to us, so NGSA alone costs only $0.64B (S2), or $0.83B on the A320 Alt plan (S3).
- Technology: no. At a 2040 EIS every engine code gives CFM only.
- So we are not ready on all three [BX-1296].
(3) What if certification takes longer than we think? Malave ran S6 as the baseline (section 4).
(4) Is this doing less, better? I compared every row against Do Nothing in the same column [BX-1239].

3. THE TESTED CASE AGAINST DO NOTHING AND S6 (Board recommendation 1)
Each row reads S1 / S2 / S3 / S4 / S5 / S6.
- Submitted, Do Nothing: 0.00 / -0.64 / -0.83 / -2.62 / -3.26 / -0.64. S6 equals Do Nothing's own S6.
- There are no Board items, so there are no default rows to show.
- Rejected rows, for the record:

airbus.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Today Airbus launches its next-generation single-aisle aircraft, with entry into service planned in the second half of the 2030s. This is how we prepare the Airbus of the 2030s: on the clock of technology maturity, with a disciplined and controlled ramp-up. To serve our customers through the transition, we will keep the A320 family in production for longer on our proven lines while the new aircraft ramps up. We have invited CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to power the new aircraft, because robust, multi-source engine supply matters to our customers and to the ramp. We will fund the programme from our own cash generation, within our financial framework, and preserve our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus. Together with our European industrial base, our suppliers and our partners worldwide, we will continue to work with the whole industry for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aviation.
airbus.rationale:
ROUND 1 (2030). DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE, ON THE BRIEF'S GRID ONLY.

Order of argument:
- Five pillars [AX-0073, AX-0081].
- A disciplined and controlled ramp [AX-0010].
- Preparing the Airbus of the 2030s on the technology clock [AX-0020, AX-0006, A-0409].
- What the Board can carry: one programme, inside a year's FCF, with no item losing more than $2B in any column [AX-0026, AX-0022, AX-0104].

1. DELETED ON RED LINES OR PILLARS, WHATEVER THEIR PV
- NGSA (base or Alt) + A350 Re-engine:
  - Rule 6: two launches in one round, with a 5-year overlap from 2030 to 2035.
  - Peak cash: $6.674B a year against $5.2B.
  - Its item value is -2.15 in S6 and S7. It is on the Board's would-veto list. This is the raw best in S1 to S5 (+15.83 in S1); it is a red-line deletion, not a premium.
- Every Delay Tactics row (bottleneck, poaching, both):
  - Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine.
  - Integrity pillar.
  - The Board vetoes bottleneck and both always, and poaching now.
  - One move is worth -15.74 in S1 and -15.75 in S6 against the lean.

2. SOFT VETOES ACCEPTED
- A350 Re-engine alone: fails Toepfer's robustness test and Wagner's A350F/Spirit absorption test. It trails the lean by $1.85B (S4) to $14.73B (S6), so no override is possible. It also gives up the last NGSA launch year.
- Alt plan with the $0.75B lumped into one development year: fails peak cash ($5.824B). Remedied by phasing it over 2037-44.

3. SURVIVORS
| Row | S1 | S2 | S3 | S4 | S5 | S6 | S7 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Do Nothing | 0.00 | -2.72 | -2.55 | -4.07 | -2.72 | -0.86 | -3.58 |
| NGSA, base plan (doctrine default) | +11.49 | +2.37 | +3.55 | -0.70 | +2.37 | +10.62 | +1.51 |
| NGSA, Alt plan, A350 hold (ordered) | +14.09 | +4.46 | +5.43 | +1.04 | +4.46 | +13.23 | +3.60 |

The ordered row is the best survivor in every column, so the choice does not depend on my scenario call. It beats the doctrine default by +2.60 / +2.09 / +1.88 / +1.74 / +2.09 / +2.61 / +2.09, more than the $1B margin in every column, so I depart from the base-plan default. Its worst column (S4 at +1.04) stays positive, which meets my robustness preference; the base plan's worst column (-0.70) does not. The within-$1B tie-breaks do not apply.

One tie-break note for the record: after a one-year slip, NGSA's EIS would be 2038, outside 2035-2037. No alternative exists, because 2030 is the last year of the 2028-2030 window and the board offers no earlier launch. Holding NGSA would give up the window, so I accept the exposure. The public window, "the second half of the 2030s", covers a one-year slip; the internal target stays 2037.

4. ITEM VALUES FOR THE BOARD, COLUMN BY COLUMN
- With each Board item at its default: the ngsa item at hold is the Do Nothing row (the Alt plan has no effect without NGSA). The a320_plan item at base is the NGSA base row.
- NGSA item against Do Nothing (base plan): +11.49 / +5.09 / +6.10 / +3.37 / +5.09 / +11.48 / +5.09.
- Alt item against the base plan: +2.60 / +2.09 / +1.88 / +1.74 / +2.09 / +2.61 / +2.09.
- Package against Do Nothing: +14.09 / +7.18 / +7.98 / +5.11 / +7.18 / +14.09 / +7.18.
- No item loses money in any column, so every item passes the Board's -$2B line.

5. BOARD-GATE LINES
- `ngsa: launch`, engine code 7 (Qualified Majority):
  - Five pillars: pass. Wagner reports no safety or quality event and no open finding.
  - Toepfer: pass. Peak cash is $5.074B a year in 2030-36 against $5.2B ($0.126B headroom), with no overlap; robustness passes.
  - Wagner: pass on engineering capacity, production readiness, safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch.
  - Grid ΔPV against Do Nothing: as above, minimum +3.37 (S4).
  - Engine sources: at a 2037 EIS, on today's record only CFM is fitted. P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) and RR UltraFan NB (ready 2037, no slack) are fitted only if they launch on our selection this round.
- `a320_plan: alt` (read with the package):
  - Five pillars: pass.
  - Toepfer: pass, with the $0.75B phased over 2037-44 and any pre-EIS commitment capped at $0.10B a year.
  - Wagner: pass on all five tests. The A320 runs at 82 a month at most, below today's 85, so this is a run-down on mature lines, not a ramp.
  - Grid ΔPV against the base plan: as above, minimum +1.74.
- `rea350: hold` and `delay_tactics: none` are defaults and are not Board items.
- No override is used, and the budget of one per game is intact.

6. DELAY TACTICS
The team's stricter Delay Tactics condition stands: the move must change who enters service first. On this board it shifts share, not EIS, so read literally it keeps Delay Tactics off. I do not set it aside. Delay Tactics are off. I would revisit only if an fps is on the public record, and then only one poaching move while NGSA is in development, with the grid showing at least $1B and every Board condition met.

7. OWN CLOCK
Boeing's posture played no part in the launch. The launch rests on the technology window and the grid. No future Boeing move will re-time or cancel NGSA (rules 2 and 7).

8. SUPPLY ATTRIBUTION
Wagner's illustrative ramp shows neither A320 plan closing the early-2040s capacity gap during the transition. The binding constraints are engines and structures at the combined peak. Hence the supply moves: A320neo engine slots, titanium and rare earths for our own ramp.

(1) Peak cash: NGSA at $35.52B over 7 development years is $5.07B a year against the $5.2B line (€4.75bn FCF at $1.10). Confirm the $0.13B headroom and the development-year profile from 2030 to 2037.
(2) The Alt plan's $0.75B: when is it spent? If it falls after the 2037 entry into service, when NGSA development spend has rolled off, the peak stays at $5.07B. Spread over development, the peak is $5.18B, which passes. Lumped into one development year, it is $5.82B, which fails. Propose a phasing that keeps every year under $5.2B, or tell me it cannot be done.
(3) Confirm that net cash (€12.2bn today [AX-0102]) still carries the 30-50% payout and the €5bn buyback with no equity raise. State support counts as upside only. Is the debt penalty already in the grid?
(4) Robustness: confirm the worst plausible column for each surviving row. As I read it, S4 is +1.04 for the lean, -0.70 for the base-plan NGSA and -4.07 for Do Nothing. Confirm the lean is positive in all seven columns.
(5) Record the cash view of NGSA plus an A350 Re-engine ($6.67B a year) as a fail. Pre-read the next rounds: does a 2035 Re-engine launch overlap NGSA by 2 years and fail the line, while a 2045 launch clears it?
(6) Draft the Board-gate lines for ngsa: launch (Qualified Majority, with the engine code) and for a320_plan alt (read with the package): five pillars, your test, Lars's test, and the grid ΔPV against Do Nothing and against the base plan, column by column.
(7) Your pass or fail on each candidate row, and whether any failure is a soft veto.
frame.asks_ops:
Lars, please bring the production, supply and quality memo.
(1) Engineering capacity: can we launch NGSA in 2030 while we run the A320 at 85 a month and absorb the A350F, without starving the ramp of engineers and suppliers [A-0366, A-0485]? The rate-75 commitment for end-2027 [AX-0054] is behind us by then. Pass or fail.
(2) The Alt plan: it keeps the A320 lines at 82, 62, 52, 42, then 14 a month for about eight years after the 2037 EIS, while NGSA ramps to 50 a month around EIS+4, 80 around +6 and 100 around +8. Give me a result on each of safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield, supply crunch (CFM and P&W A320neo engines plus the NGSA engines and structures at the combined peak) and production readiness. Then give me the same five results for NGSA on the base plan. The Board accepts no override of the first four, so a fail means base.
(3) Capacity against demand: on the conservative curve we are capacity-bound from 2035, and Boeing takes our slack. Does the Alt plan, together with our 1% capacity creep while short, close that gap in the 2040s? Is there a concrete constraint (engines, titanium, rare earths [AX-0062, AX-0063]) we should secure first?
(4) Engine code: your supply recommendation among 5, 6 and 7. GTF2 launched in 2030 would be ready in 2036. UltraFan NB would be ready in 2037, which is our EIS year with no slack. A maker that is not ready is dropped, and NGSA does not wait. Code 7 is in no barred pair. Do you see any reason not to name all three [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360]?
(5) Confirm the A350 stays on hold in round 1 (A350F absorption [AX-0082]), and give your pre-read on a later Re-engine window.
(6) Flag any order whose public explanation would contradict the five pillars.
frame.initial_lean:
My lean: ngsa launch in 2030 (EIS 2037, "around 2037", in "the second half of the next decade" [A-0409, AX-0020]); ngsa_engine_code 7, subject to Lars's supply recommendation; a320_plan alt, if Lars passes it on safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch and Thomas phases the $0.75B to keep every year under $5.2B; rea350 hold; delay_tactics none.

On the grid this row reads +14.09 / +4.46 / +5.43 / +1.04 / +4.46 / +13.23 / +3.60. It is the best surviving row in every column, so my choice does not depend on which scenario I expect. My working expectation is S1: Boeing holds this round, given its stated preconditions and our prior of no fps before the next round. S4 (fps 7-yr, same EIS year, Boeing climbing toward 50%) is the worst plausible column at +1.04, still positive. Against Do Nothing, NGSA gains in every column (+3.37 to +11.49 on the base plan). The Alt plan adds a further $1.74B to $2.61B in every column, more than the $1B doctrine margin, so I depart from the base-plan doctrine default unless a test fails. If Lars fails the Alt plan, I take the base plan (worst column S4 at -0.70) without override, because the Board accepts none there.

The raw best plan, Alt plus an A350 Re-engine, scores $1.74B more in S1-S5. It is deleted on rule 6, on peak cash ($6.67B) and on the Board's veto, and it is not a premium I am paying for doctrine. The A350 Re-engine waits until NGSA spend rolls off, on its own test in a later round, and never after a 787 Re-engine.

Delay Tactics stay off: no fps is public, the fine for a naked move is $48.32B, it fails integrity, and the team's stricter condition stands. I will record that in the rationale.

Ordering logic: the five pillars first [AX-0073, AX-0081]; a disciplined and controlled ramp [AX-0010]; preparing the Airbus of the 2030s on the technology clock [AX-0020, AX-0006]; then taking it to the Board as one programme within a year's FCF [AX-0026, AX-0022, AX-0104]. Board items: ngsa launch with the engine code (Qualified Majority), and the Alt plan read with the package. No override is planned.

tests.name: Peak annual cash: NGSA launched 2030, base A320 plan (ask 1)
tests.threshold: Peak annual programme cash spend no higher than about one year's FCF: €4,753m x $1.10 = $5.228B, line taken at $5.2B (game guardrail, inference)
tests.numbers: $35.52B / 7 development years = $5.074B a year in each of 2030-2036, EIS 2037. The board books the bill at EIS; this is the cash view, spread evenly. Headroom is $0.126B against $5.2B ($0.154B against the unrounded $5.228B). NGSA development spend is $0 from 2037. No strain while the A350 is on hold. Any other spend above $0.126B in a 2030-36 year breaks the line.

tests.name: Peak annual cash: A320 Alt plan, phasing of the $0.75B (ask 2)
tests.threshold: Every year 2030-2036 at or below $5.2B with the Alt cost added
tests.numbers: Proposed phasing: spend the $0.75B as the longer A320 lines run after EIS, 2037-2044, about $0.094B a year. Peak stays $5.074B (2030-36), and programme spend in 2037-44 is about $0.09B a year. If any pre-EIS commitment is needed, cap it at $0.10B in any 2030-36 year, inside the $0.126B headroom. Spread evenly over 2030-36: $5.074B + $0.107B = $5.181B, a pass by $0.019B with no buffer; not recommended. Lumped into one development year: $5.824B, a fail by $0.624B. The grid does not show the timing (supply-plan cost valued at WACC, no debt penalty), so the Board paper must fix it.

tests.name: Peak annual cash: NGSA plus A350 Re-engine both launched 2030 (ask 5)
tests.threshold: At or below $5.2B a year
tests.numbers: NGSA $5.074B + Re-engine $5B / 5 = $1.0B + strain $3B x 5/5 overlap years / 5 = $0.6B, giving $6.674B a year in 2030-2034. With the Alt cost spread over development it is $6.781B. That is $1.47B to $1.58B over the line.

tests.name: Peak annual cash: A350 Re-engine without NGSA
tests.threshold: At or below $5.2B a year
tests.numbers: $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year, 2030-2034, no strain. It passes on cash but fails robustness (below).

tests.name: Overlap and one-launch rule: NGSA / A350 Re-engine, with the pre-read for later rounds (ask 5)
tests.threshold: At most one new launch per round; NGSA / A350 Re-engine development overlap of 2 years or less unless the grid shows at least $1B more (rule 6, red line)
tests.numbers: Concurrent 2030 launch: NGSA development 2030-2037 and Re-engine 2030-2035 give 5 overlap years, and two launches in one round. The Re-engine item over the lean is +1.74/+1.75/+1.74/+1.74/+1.75/-2.15/-2.15 (S1-S7), so not at least $1B in S6-S7. Red line, deleted. Pre-read: a Re-engine launched in 2035 (development 2035-2040) overlaps NGSA by 2 years (2035-36). That passes the overlap limit but fails cash: $5.074B + $1.0B + $0.6B (strain $3B x 2/5 over 2 years) = $6.674B in 2035 and 2036. A 2045 launch (development 2045-2050) does not overlap: $1.0B a year, which passes cash. It still needs its own robustness test then, and rule 3 bars it if a 787 Re-engine is public.

tests.name: Net cash, payout and buyback: the Board's liquidity line (ask 3)
tests.threshold: Net cash kept; the 30-50% payout and the €5bn buyback fundable with no equity raise (Board line, inference)
tests.numbers: Net cash €12.2bn = $13.42B. The €5bn buyback runs over three years from July 2026 and completes by 2029, before the first NGSA development year. FY2025 dividend: about 48% x €5,221m net income = €2.5bn, or $2.76B. Stress case (FCF flat at FY2025's $5.228B, NGSA fully incremental): $0.154B a year is left after NGSA. At a 48% payout net cash falls about $2.6B a year: about $0.4B at end-2034 and -$4.8B by 2036. At the 30% floor ($1.72B) it falls to about $2.4B in 2036 and stays positive. On the board's own path, operating profit is $6.4-7.7B a year in 2030-36 against $3.6B in 2026 (1.8-2.1x), so FCF should beat the stress case (inference). No equity raise in either case. State support and refundable advances count as upside only. The debt penalty is in the grid (debt $10B, alpha 0.30, about $1.2B before discounting for NGSA); the Alt cost carries none.

tests.threshold: Within $1B, prefer fewer Board items and the later capex start
tests.numbers: The lean carries 2 Board items (ngsa launch; a320_plan alt), the base plan 1. The Alt plan is $1.74B-$2.61B ahead, outside the $1B band, so the tie-break does not bite. NGSA in 2030 is the last window year. The Alt cost phased after EIS is the later capex start.

tests.threshold: Disclosure only: lead with the grid, never hide a charge

Before any offset, it would move S4 to about -2.4 for the base-plan NGSA item and about -0.6 for the lean against Do Nothing; S1 stays at about +5.8 and +8.4. tests.threshold: Pass or fail on each row, and whether a failure is a soft veto or a red line
tests.numbers: Do Nothing: no cash fail; worst S4 -4.07; gives up the last NGSA year (Faury's call, not a cash test). NGSA base: passes all. Lean: passes all, on the Alt phasing condition. NGSA (base or Alt) + A350 Re-engine: fails peak cash, overlap and robustness; red line rule 6, binding. A350 Re-engine alone: fails robustness; soft veto, binding, and it trails the lean by at least $1.85B. Any Delay Tactics row: fails fine exposure, and `both` also fails the second-move test; red line rule 4, binding. Alt plan with the $0.75B lumped into one development year: fails peak cash; soft veto, binding, margin 0.00 against the phased version.

vetoes.plan: NGSA (base or Alt plan) plus rea350 launch in 2030
vetoes.ground: Red line, rule 6: two new launches in one round with a 5-year development overlap (2030-2035), and the Re-engine item is -2.15 in S6 and S7, so not at least $1B. It also fails peak cash ($6.674B a year, $6.781B with the Alt cost spread, against $5.2B) and robustness. Grid margin against the best passing option (the lean): +1.74/+1.75/+1.74/+1.74/+1.75/-2.15/-2.15. Deleted whatever its PV; no override can restore it.

vetoes.ground: Failed robustness test: item against Do Nothing is -0.64 in S6 and S7. Soft veto. Grid margin against the best passing option (the lean): -10.83/-3.92/-4.72/-1.85/-3.92/-14.73/-7.82, so it is behind in every column and the $1B override test cannot be met.

vetoes.ground: Red line, rule 4: no fps is on the public record, so any move is naked against a $48.32B fine. `both` is a second move and buys nothing (-0.51 to -0.63 over one move). `bottleneck` is also an integrity flag under the five pillars that I could not defend to the Audit Committee. One move is worth -15.74/-0.27/-0.41/-0.31/-0.27/-15.75/-0.28 against the lean. Not overridable.

vetoes.plan: a320_plan alt with its $0.75B lumped into a single NGSA development year (2030-2036)
vetoes.ground: Failed peak-cash test: $5.074B + $0.75B = $5.824B against $5.2B. Soft veto. Grid margin against the best passing option (the same Alt plan phased after EIS, 2037-44): 0.00 in every column, so no override can meet $1B. Remedy: phase the spend after EIS, or cap it at $0.10B in any development year.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: I would move from the lean to NGSA on the base plan in two cases: (1) Lars fails the Alt plan on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield or supply crunch; or (2) the $0.75B cannot be kept to $0.126B or less in every 2030-36 year. NGSA alone still passes all my tests ($5.074B a year; item +3.37 to +11.49). I would change the package if the grid showed an option at least $1B better than the lean in every plausible column that also passed peak cash, or if the Board decided otherwise. On liquidity, I would take a payout reset to the Board, never an equity raise, if 2030-36 FCF tracked below FY2025's €4,753m with no offset, so that even the 30% floor drew net cash below zero. If the Board asks for the cash-timed view (bill spread over 2030-36 rather than booked at EIS), the base-plan NGSA item reads about -2.4 in S4, beyond its -$2B line, while the lean stays about -0.6. That makes the Alt plan more important, not less. A public fps or 787 Re-engine next round does not reopen NGSA (rules 2 and 7). It does re-run Delay Tactics fine exposure, and robustness and the rule-3 check for any A350 Re-engine; a 2035 Re-engine still fails cash at $6.674B in 2035-36.
cfo.memo:
Round 1 (2030), on the brief's grid. Recommended: ngsa launch, engine code 7 (I defer to Lars on the code), a320_plan alt, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none.

Peak cash. NGSA is $35.52B over seven development years, 2030-36: $5.07B a year against the $5.2B line (FCF of €4,753m at $1.10). Headroom $0.13B. Pass, narrowly; nothing else can enter development beside it.

Alt plan. Spend the $0.75B as the longer A320 lines run, 2037-44, about $0.09B a year, after NGSA spend rolls off: the peak stays $5.07B. Spread over development it is $5.18B, a pass with no buffer; lumped into one year, $5.82B, a fail. The Board paper should fix that phasing.

Robustness. All seven columns count. The lean row is +1.04 at worst (S4) and gains +5.11 to +14.09 on Do Nothing. NGSA on the base plan gains +3.37 to +11.49. The Alt plan adds +1.74 to +2.61 in every column, above the $1B premium.

Net cash. The €5bn buyback runs off by 2029, before NGSA spend. No equity raise. On flat FY2025 FCF, a 48% payout takes net cash to about nil by 2034; the 30% floor keeps it positive. State support is upside only. The debt penalty is in the grid.

Disclosure: the grid books NGSA at EIS; cash leaves in 2030-36, about $5.7B of PV at 8% the grid does not charge.

Deleted: an A350 Re-engine beside NGSA ($6.67B a year, rule 6, -2.15 in S6-S7); the Re-engine alone (-0.64); any Delay Tactics (naked $48.32B fine).

tests.name: Engineering capacity: NGSA alone (2030 launch, A350 on hold) [Faury ask 1]
tests.threshold: Rule 6 allows one new launch per round. NGSA/A350 development overlap must be 2 years or less ($1.2B strain), unless the grid shows at least $1B more.
tests.numbers: NGSA development runs 2030-2037: $35.52B, or $5.07B a year. The A350 is held, so overlap is 0 years and strain is $0. The A320 runs at a steady 85 a month (capacity 1,020 a year). It delivers 852 in 2030 and 951 in 2032, and is capacity-bound only from 2034-35. That is sustaining engineering, not a ramp, so a 2030 launch does not starve the line of engineers or suppliers. The end-2027 rate commitment is behind us.

tests.name: Engineering capacity and rule 6: NGSA + A350 Re-engine both launched in 2030
tests.threshold: Rule 6 allows one new launch per round. NGSA/A350 development overlap must be 2 years or less, unless the grid shows at least $1B more.
tests.numbers: Two new launches in one round. NGSA develops 2030-2037 and the A350 Re-engine 2030-2035: a 5-year overlap, $3.0B of strain ($0.6B a year), $6.67B a year in the overlap years. Against the best passing row (NGSA Alt + A350 hold) the grid gives +1.74 / +1.75 / +1.74 / +1.74 / +1.75 / -2.15 / -2.15 (S1-S7). That is not $1B or more in every column. Two launches in one round is a red line whatever the margin.

tests.name: A350F and Spirit A350 absorption: A350 on hold in round 1 [Faury ask 5]
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 work packages are being absorbed: not in round 1 (2030), round 2 (2035) at the earliest.
tests.numbers: rea350 hold is confirmed. Pre-read for round 2: a 2035 launch (EIS 2040) overlaps NGSA development in 2035-37. That is 2 years and $1.2B of strain ($0.6B a year), exactly at my limit, and it passes only if no supply crunch is reported. Its EIS also lands at NGSA EIS+3, inside the ramp to 50 a month. On cash it means $6.67B a year in 2035-36, which is Toepfer's test. A launch in the 2045 round has no overlap. Never after a 787 Re-engine (rule 3).

tests.name: A350F and Spirit A350 absorption: any A350 Re-engine launch in 2030, with or without NGSA
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine in round 1.
tests.numbers: The A350 Re-engine alone scores +3.26 / +0.54 / +0.71 / -0.81 / +0.54 / -1.50 / -4.22. It trails the best passing row by $1.85B (S4) to $14.73B (S6), so no $1B override can apply. It also gives up the last NGSA launch year. For the version with NGSA, see the rule 6 entry.

tests.name: Production readiness: NGSA launch in 2030, base and Alt plans [Faury ask 2]
tests.threshold: Launch inside the 2028-2030 window, once the wing is buildable at rate and the production system has matured with the aircraft. Rule 1: no EIS before 2035.
tests.numbers: Launch in 2030, the last year of the window. EIS 2037 is 2 years after the 2035 technology-ready year. NGSA ramp anchors are 50 a month at EIS+4 (2041), 80 at +6 (2043) and 100 at +8 (2045). On the base plan the A320 winds down 72, 52, 42, 14, then none about 5 years after EIS, which bets on NGSA hitting its anchors. On the Alt plan it runs 82, 62, 52, 42, then 14 for about 8 years in all: about 1,500 more A320s on proven lines. That hedges the 1-2 years of ramp slip our own record shows (rate 75 slipped about 2 years). Both plans pass, and Alt is the more robust production plan.

tests.name: Safety: NGSA launch, base and Alt plans [Faury ask 2]
tests.threshold: Five pillars: no order that compromises safety. Never overridden.
tests.numbers: The brief reports no safety event, and no order touches an open safety finding. The Alt plan runs existing, certified A320 lines longer at lower rates (82 a month at most after EIS).

tests.name: Quality, and public explanations: base and Alt plans [Faury asks 2 and 6]
tests.threshold: No order whose public explanation would contradict safety and quality.
tests.numbers: In public the Alt plan reads as extended A320 family production through the NGSA transition, which is consistent with the pillars. Quality watch: the 14-a-month tail runs about 4 years (around 2041-44) while staff move to NGSA, so consolidate it on the fewest lines to keep skills. Flags: no Delay Tactics move can be explained publicly. Give NGSA EIS and rates as windows ('second half of the 2030s'), not dates. Publish no 2040s A320 rate numbers.

tests.name: A320 ramp shield: base and Alt plans [Faury ask 2]
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with the open A320 ramp commitment. On this board it passes unless the brief reports a ramp problem.
tests.numbers: The end-2027 commitment (70-75 a month, then 75) is behind us. The A320 runs at 85 a month (capacity 1,020 a year), and no ramp problem is reported. After EIS the Alt plan holds the A320 at 82 a month or less, never above today's rate, for about $0.75B. Phasing that $0.75B under the $5.2B line is Toepfer's test.

tests.name: Supply crunch: base and Alt plans (CFM and P&W A320neo engines, plus NGSA engines and structures at the combined peak) [Faury ask 2]
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch, no new concurrency.
tests.numbers: No crunch is reported, so the trigger does not fire. Forward check: today's 85 a month needs 2,040 engines a year (CFM 1,224, P&W 816 at 60/40). The Alt tail peaks at 82 a month (1,968 engines a year), then falls to 14 a month (336 a year). That is a run-down, not a ramp. My straight-line reading of the rules' ramp anchors (illustrative, not a board number): Alt runs about 64-82 a month in 2037-42 and peaks around 104 in 2044 (90 NGSA + 14 A320). Base runs about 52-72 a month in 2037-42 and reaches 100 in 2045. Both carry about 9-10% of capacity creep on top. Alt's peak is about 4% above base, and the extra 14 a month are on mature lines. Secure first: A320neo tail engine slots (CFM, P&W), NGSA engines at CFM (the only certain maker), titanium and rare earths.

tests.name: Capacity against demand [Faury ask 3; for information, not a veto test]
tests.threshold: Report only.
tests.numbers: Do Nothing: capacity-bound from 2035 at 1,020 a year, creeping to 1,127. In 2045 we would want 1,211 (60% of 2,019) against 1,105 of capacity, and the whole market has 1,789 slots (1,105 + 684) against 2,019 demand. With NGSA our preference rises 1 pp a year from 2037 (about 63% in 2040, 68% in 2045), so we would want about 1,135 in 2040 and 1,373 in 2045. On my illustrative ramp, base supplies about 650 and Alt about 1,000 in 2040. In 2045 both supply about 1,330 (100 a month with creep). Neither plan closes the gap in the early 2040s. Alt narrows it most in 2037-44, and the gap nearly closes around 2045. The brief has no supply table for the NGSA rows. The grid's Alt item (+1.74 to +2.61 in every column) confirms the extra A320s sell.

tests.name: Engine supply: NGSA engine code (a recommendation, not a veto ground) [Faury ask 4]
tests.threshold: CFM plus at least one second maker (code 5, 6 or 7). Code 7 when I cannot tell which maker will be ready by NGSA EIS.
tests.numbers:
Readiness by the 2037 EIS:
- CFM: always ready.
- P&W GTF2: if launched in 2030, ready in 2036 (1 year of slack).
- Joint Venture: if formed in 2030, ready in 2036.
- RR UltraFan NB: if launched in 2030, ready in 2037 (no slack).
An engine launched in the 2035 round would be ready only in 2041-42, too late for 2037, so only a 2030 selection can add a second source at EIS. 2050 metric: 1/1 if the makers hold (CFM alone, against 2/2 on Do Nothing); 3/3 on code 7 if both launch. Code 7 is in no barred pair. I recommend code 7. Operating cost the board does not price: up to three engine integrations in 2030-37 on teams that already bind. An unready maker is dropped, so NGSA never waits (rule 8 cannot bind).

tests.name: Engine maturity slip
tests.threshold: If the brief reports one, re-time NGSA so EIS stays at or after the new technology-ready year. Never cancel.
tests.numbers: No slip is reported in the brief.

tests.name: Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No reaction: we keep our own disciplined ramp.
tests.numbers: No Boeing move is on the public record. The MAX runs at 57 a month from 2030. This changes none of our programmes.

tests.name: Delay Tactics, any move in 2030 (rules 4-5, five pillars, team's stricter condition)
tests.threshold: No move before an fps is launched. At most one move (`both` is two). `poaching` only while a programme is in development. `bottleneck` only as a first claim on capacity for our own ramp.
tests.numbers: No fps is on the public record, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine. One move on the lean scores -15.74 / -0.27 / -0.41 / -0.31 / -0.27 / -15.75 / -0.28 against it. `both` scores -16.26 to -0.83. Neither changes who enters service first. The recommended order, `none`, passes.

vetoes.plan: rea350: launch alongside ngsa: launch, on either the base or the Alt A320 plan
vetoes.ground: Company red line rule 6, which cannot be overridden: two new launches in one round, with a 5-year NGSA/A350 development overlap (2030-2035), $3B of strain and $6.67B a year in the overlap years. It also fails my A350F and Spirit A350 absorption test, a soft veto. Grid margin against the best passing row (NGSA Alt + A350 hold): +1.74 / +1.75 in S1-S5 and -2.15 in S6-S7.

vetoes.plan: rea350: launch with ngsa: hold (the A350 Re-engine alone in 2030)
vetoes.ground: It fails my A350F and Spirit A350 absorption test (no A350 Re-engine in round 1), a soft veto. Grid margin against the best passing row: -10.83 / -3.92 / -4.72 / -1.85 / -3.92 / -14.73 / -7.82, so it can never clear the $1B override test. It also gives up the last NGSA launch year.

vetoes.plan: delay_tactics: bottleneck, poaching or both (any move this round)
vetoes.ground: Company red line rule 4: no Delay Tactics before an fps is launched (none is public), and `both` is a second move. `bottleneck` and `both` also breach the five pillars (integrity). Any move is naked against the $48.32B fine and scores -15.74 (S1), -15.75 (S6) and -0.27 to -0.41 elsewhere against the lean. It fails the team's stricter condition too, because it does not change who enters service first.

ops.memo:
My tests are role-derived (Very low confidence). None of this is in my own recorded words.

NGSA in 2030 passes. EIS 2037 comes after the 2035 technology-ready year. With the A350 on hold, NGSA overlaps nothing: zero years, zero strain. The rate-75 date (end-2027) is behind us, and no ramp problem or supply crunch is reported.

The Alt plan passes on safety, quality, the ramp shield, supply crunch and readiness, and I prefer it. Its A320 lines never exceed 82 a month, below today's 85, so CFM and P&W see a slower run-down, not a ramp. On the base plan our combined rate falls well below 85 a month while NGSA climbs to 50. Alt fills much of that trough with about 1,500 A320s, and it insures us if our ramp slips, as rate 75 did. First secure A320neo engines for the tail, and titanium and rare earths for the combined peak around 2044.

Engine code 7. GTF2 would be ready in 2036, UltraFan NB in 2037 with no slack. I cannot tell which maker will launch, and only a 2030 selection gets either in by EIS. Otherwise NGSA flies CFM alone by 2050.

Binding vetoes: an A350 Re-engine in 2030, with or without NGSA, fails A350F absorption. With NGSA it also breaks rule 6: two launches, a five-year overlap, $3B of strain and -$2.15B in S6-S7. Any Delay Tactics breaks rule 4, because no fps is public.

In public: windows, not dates, and a disciplined and controlled ramp.

other_moves.move: Secure our own supply for the transition
other_moves.detail: Long-term agreements for A320neo engine slots with CFM and P&W to cover the longer A320 tail, and NGSA engines from CFM, the only maker certain to be ready. Titanium and rare-earth supply secured for the combined A320/NGSA peak in the mid-2040s, the follow-on to the 2025 de-risking [AX-0062, AX-0063]. These are for our own ramp. No action is aimed at any rival's supply chain.

other_moves.move: Engineering recruitment for the Airbus of the 2030s
other_moves.detail: Normal hiring and internal redeployment to staff NGSA development, sized so the A320 sustaining teams and the A350F are not stripped [A-0366, A-0485]. This is not targeted at any competitor's programme and is not a Delay Tactics move.

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
other_moves.detail: Continue to work through industry coalitions for a tariff-free regime for civil aircraft and parts [AX-0088].

other_moves.move: Consolidate the A320 tail on the fewest lines (Wagner's quality watch)
other_moves.detail: Under the Alt plan the 14-a-month tail runs about four years while staff move to NGSA. Concentrate it on the fewest lines to keep skills and quality. Publish no A320 rate numbers for the 2040s.

other_moves.move: Board paper fixes the phasing of the Alt plan's $0.75B
other_moves.detail: Spend about $0.094B a year in 2037-44 as the longer A320 lines run, after NGSA development spend rolls off. Any pre-EIS commitment is capped at $0.10B in any 2030-36 year, inside the $0.126B headroom. Peak programme cash stays at $5.074B a year against the $5.2B line.

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Today Airbus launches its next-generation single-aisle aircraft, with entry into service planned in the second half of the 2030s. This is how we prepare the Airbus of the 2030s: on the clock of technology maturity, with a disciplined and controlled ramp-up. To serve our customers through the transition, we will keep the A320 family in production for longer on our proven lines while the new aircraft ramps up. We have invited CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to power the new aircraft, because robust, multi-source engine supply matters to our customers and to the ramp. We will fund the programme from our own cash generation, within our financial framework, and preserve our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus. Together with our European industrial base, our suppliers and our partners worldwide, we will continue to work with the whole industry for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aviation.
decision.rationale:
ROUND 1 (2030). DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE, ON THE BRIEF'S GRID ONLY.

Order of argument:
- Five pillars [AX-0073, AX-0081].
- A disciplined and controlled ramp [AX-0010].
- Preparing the Airbus of the 2030s on the technology clock [AX-0020, AX-0006, A-0409].
- What the Board can carry: one programme, inside a year's FCF, with no item losing more than $2B in any column [AX-0026, AX-0022, AX-0104].

1. DELETED ON RED LINES OR PILLARS, WHATEVER THEIR PV
- NGSA (base or Alt) + A350 Re-engine:
  - Rule 6: two launches in one round, with a 5-year overlap from 2030 to 2035.
  - Peak cash: $6.674B a year against $5.2B.
  - Its item value is -2.15 in S6 and S7. It is on the Board's would-veto list. This is the raw best in S1 to S5 (+15.83 in S1); it is a red-line deletion, not a premium.
- Every Delay Tactics row (bottleneck, poaching, both):
  - Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine.
  - Integrity pillar.
  - The Board vetoes bottleneck and both always, and poaching now.
  - One move is worth -15.74 in S1 and -15.75 in S6 against the lean.

2. SOFT VETOES ACCEPTED
- A350 Re-engine alone: fails Toepfer's robustness test and Wagner's A350F/Spirit absorption test. It trails the lean by $1.85B (S4) to $14.73B (S6), so no override is possible. It also gives up the last NGSA launch year.
- Alt plan with the $0.75B lumped into one development year: fails peak cash ($5.824B). Remedied by phasing it over 2037-44.

3. SURVIVORS
| Row | S1 | S2 | S3 | S4 | S5 | S6 | S7 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Do Nothing | 0.00 | -2.72 | -2.55 | -4.07 | -2.72 | -0.86 | -3.58 |
| NGSA, base plan (doctrine default) | +11.49 | +2.37 | +3.55 | -0.70 | +2.37 | +10.62 | +1.51 |
| NGSA, Alt plan, A350 hold (ordered) | +14.09 | +4.46 | +5.43 | +1.04 | +4.46 | +13.23 | +3.60 |

The ordered row is the best survivor in every column, so the choice does not depend on my scenario call. It beats the doctrine default by +2.60 / +2.09 / +1.88 / +1.74 / +2.09 / +2.61 / +2.09, more than the $1B margin in every column, so I depart from the base-plan default. Its worst column (S4 at +1.04) stays positive, which meets my robustness preference; the base plan's worst column (-0.70) does not. The within-$1B tie-breaks do not apply.

One tie-break note for the record: after a one-year slip, NGSA's EIS would be 2038, outside 2035-2037. No alternative exists, because 2030 is the last year of the 2028-2030 window and the board offers no earlier launch. Holding NGSA would give up the window, so I accept the exposure. The public window, "the second half of the 2030s", covers a one-year slip; the internal target stays 2037.

4. ITEM VALUES FOR THE BOARD, COLUMN BY COLUMN
- With each Board item at its default: the ngsa item at hold is the Do Nothing row (the Alt plan has no effect without NGSA). The a320_plan item at base is the NGSA base row.
- NGSA item against Do Nothing (base plan): +11.49 / +5.09 / +6.10 / +3.37 / +5.09 / +11.48 / +5.09.
- Alt item against the base plan: +2.60 / +2.09 / +1.88 / +1.74 / +2.09 / +2.61 / +2.09.
- Package against Do Nothing: +14.09 / +7.18 / +7.98 / +5.11 / +7.18 / +14.09 / +7.18.
- No item loses money in any column, so every item passes the Board's -$2B line.

5. BOARD-GATE LINES
- `ngsa: launch`, engine code 7 (Qualified Majority):
  - Five pillars: pass. Wagner reports no safety or quality event and no open finding.
  - Toepfer: pass. Peak cash is $5.074B a year in 2030-36 against $5.2B ($0.126B headroom), with no overlap; robustness passes.
  - Wagner: pass on engineering capacity, production readiness, safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch.
  - Grid ΔPV against Do Nothing: as above, minimum +3.37 (S4).
  - Engine sources: at a 2037 EIS, on today's record only CFM is fitted. P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) and RR UltraFan NB (ready 2037, no slack) are fitted only if they launch on our selection this round.
- `a320_plan: alt` (read with the package):
  - Five pillars: pass.
  - Toepfer: pass, with the $0.75B phased over 2037-44 and any pre-EIS commitment capped at $0.10B a year.
  - Wagner: pass on all five tests. The A320 runs at 82 a month at most, below today's 85, so this is a run-down on mature lines, not a ramp.
  - Grid ΔPV against the base plan: as above, minimum +1.74.
- `rea350: hold` and `delay_tactics: none` are defaults and are not Board items.
- No override is used, and the budget of one per game is intact.

6. DELAY TACTICS
The team's stricter Delay Tactics condition stands: the move must change who enters service first. On this board it shifts share, not EIS, so read literally it keeps Delay Tactics off. I do not set it aside. Delay Tactics are off. I would revisit only if an fps is on the public record, and then only one poaching move while NGSA is in development, with the grid showing at least $1B and every Board condition met.

7. OWN CLOCK
Boeing's posture played no part in the launch. The launch rests on the technology window and the grid. No future Boeing move will re-time or cancel NGSA (rules 2 and 7).

8. SUPPLY ATTRIBUTION
Wagner's illustrative ramp shows neither A320 plan closing the early-2040s capacity gap during the transition. The binding constraints are engines and structures at the combined peak. Hence the supply moves: A320neo engine slots, titanium and rare earths for our own ramp.

9. RECORDED GAPS
- Toepfer's cash-timing disclosure: the grid books NGSA at EIS. In a cash-timed view, before any offset, the base-plan NGSA item would be about -2.4 in S4 and the lean about -0.6 against Do Nothing. That is a further reason for the Alt plan.
- At a 48% payout on flat FY2025 FCF, net cash would approach nil around 2034. I would take a payout reset toward the 30% floor to the Board, never an equity raise.
- The Board reads the grid as given, and so do I. Both points go in the Audit Committee paper.

Doctrine premium: $0B.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Toepfer's tests are role-derived (Low confidence).

Passed for the ordered package:
- Peak cash for NGSA: $5.074B against $5.2B, $0.126B headroom.
- Alt plan: passes when the $0.75B is phased over 2037-44 (about $0.094B a year), with any pre-EIS commitment capped at $0.10B a year.
- Net cash, payout and buyback, with no equity raise: net cash €12.2bn; the buyback completes by 2029; state support counts as upside only; the debt penalty is in the grid.
- Robustness: the lean is positive in all seven columns, worst S4 at +1.04.
- The Board's downside line: item minimums are +3.37 for NGSA and +1.74 for the Alt plan.

Failed, and binding:
- NGSA + A350 Re-engine: peak cash $6.674B, rule 6, and -2.15 in S6 and S7. A red line; deleted.
- A350 Re-engine alone: fails robustness. A soft veto; it trails the lean by at least $1.85B. Accepted.
- Any Delay Tactics: rule 4, fine exposure. A red line; deleted.
- Alt plan with the $0.75B lumped into one year: fails at $5.824B. A soft veto, accepted by adopting his phasing.

I took his recommended orders in full, with no override.

I also took two disclosures into the Board paper:
- The cash-timing gap: the grid books NGSA at EIS, about $5.7B of PV uncharged before the debt-penalty offset.
- The payout stress case: a reset toward the 30% floor goes to the Board, never an equity raise.

The cash-timing gap does not change the decision, because the Board and I test on the grid. It strengthens the case for the Alt plan over the base plan.
memo_weighing.ops:
Wagner's tests are role-derived (Very low confidence).

Passed for NGSA on both the base and Alt plans:
- Engineering capacity (zero overlap, A350 on hold)
- Production readiness (EIS 2037 is after the 2035 technology-ready year)
- Safety
- Quality
- A320 ramp shield (the end-2027 commitment is behind us; no ramp problem reported)
- Supply crunch (none reported; the Alt tail is a run-down at 82 a month or less)

He passed the A350 hold on A350F and Spirit absorption, and recommended engine code 7, which I took. The code has no payoff effect, and only a 2030 selection can bring a second source in by 2037.

Failed, and binding:
- Any A350 Re-engine in 2030: with NGSA it is rule 6, a red line; alone it is his absorption test, a soft veto that trails the lean by at least $1.85B.
- Any Delay Tactics: rule 4, a red line, and integrity.

All of these I accepted.

I adopted his quality watch: consolidate the 14-a-month tail on the fewest lines, publish no 2040s A320 rates, and give windows, not dates. I also took his supply-first list into other moves: A320neo engine slots, NGSA engines from CFM, titanium and rare earths.

His capacity reading informs the objective note: neither plan closes the early-2040s gap, but the Alt plan narrows it most.

His change-of-mind triggers carry into round 2. A quality escape, safety event or A320neo engine crunch would send us back to the base plan; an engine maturity slip would re-time NGSA, never cancel it.

Boeing's own stated preconditions for a new airplane (a 20-30% gain, 'not before 2035', a repaired balance sheet) and our prior of no fps before the next round point to a hold this round [profile §7]. Working weights: S1 55%, S2 10%, S3 5%, S4 10%, S5 5%, S6 10%, S7 5%. A 737 Rate Increase is possible but is not a grid column, and we would not react to it. The ordered row is the best survivor in every column, so the call does not change the orders.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: Raw best in S1: NGSA (A320 Alt plan) + A350 Re-engine at +15.83. It is deleted on rule 6 (two launches, a 5-year overlap), on peak cash ($6.674B against $5.2B) and on the Board's veto. Best surviving plan in S1, and the one ordered: NGSA (A320 Alt plan) + A350: hold, no Delay Tactics, at +14.09. It is also the best survivor in S2 to S7.

The $1.74B gap in S1 to the raw best (adding an A350 Re-engine) is a red-line deletion under rule 6, peak cash and the Board's veto. It is not a premium traded for doctrine.
decision.objective_note:
Briefing goal: 'Defend 60/40; protect the A320 family; stable engine supply'. It is scored by the GM, and I trade no PV for it.

Defend 60/40 (preference ≥60% in 2040, 2045 and 2050):
- Do Nothing fails it: 58.4% in 2040 and 54.7% in 2045, as Boeing takes our capacity slack.
- With NGSA in service from 2037 and no fps in service, Boeing loses 1 pp a year. Customers would want about 63% from us in 2040 and 68% in 2045.
- The brief gives no share table for NGSA rows, and the slack floor applies. On Wagner's illustrative ramp, 2040 is at risk on either plan because of the transition trough. The Alt plan narrows it most (about 1,000 deliveries against about 650 on the base plan). 2045 and 2050 should be met as NGSA reaches about 100 a month with capacity creep.

Protect the A320 family (≥60% in every listed year before NGSA EIS):
- Likely not met. In 2035 our preference is 58.7%, because the firm backlog runs out while we are capacity-bound at 1,020 a year. No order this round acts before 2037.

Stable engine supply:
- In 2050, with NGSA: 1 source / 1 maker if P&W and Rolls-Royce hold; 3 / 3 on code 7 if both launch on our selection. Do Nothing gives 2 / 2.
- Code 7 is the only route to three makers and costs nothing on the grid.

Next bulletin: NGSA launched, EIS 2037, code 7, and the Alt supply plan public.

Payoff:

- In S1: +14.09.
- Range: +1.04 (S4) to +14.09 (S1).

board_response.response:
Taken up.

It does not mention Delay Tactics.

recommendations.text: Fix the phasing of the Alt plan in the Board paper and hold the ExCo to it. Spend the $0.75B in 2037-44, with at most $0.10B in any year from 2030 to 2036. All non-NGSA programme commitments in a development year, including any prepayments under the engine, titanium and rare-earth long-term agreements, must stay within the $0.126B headroom in total. If the agreements need prepayment, move all Alt spend after EIS rather than breach the line. Any lumped or advanced Alt spend returns to the Board.

With $0.126B of headroom, the Audit Committee should review NGSA's cash profile against the $5.2B line at each scheduled review of top risks. If there is an overrun or a slip, bring it to the Board with options: re-phasing, and the payout set within the 30-50% range. Never an equity raise. State support and refundable advances count as upside only, never as part of the case.

Returns: the Board notes the CFO's stress case. A 48% payout on flat FY2025 FCF takes net cash to about nil by 2034. The Board will set each year's dividend within the 30-50% range with the NGSA cash path in view. The brief's operating profit of $6.4-7.6B a year in 2030-36, against $3.6B in 2026, suggests the stress case is conservative. Show the cash-timed view (bill spread over 2030-36) alongside the grid in the Audit Committee paper.

Engine supply: the Board endorses code 7. On today's record only CFM is fitted at a 2037 EIS, and the 2050 metric is 1 / 1 if P&W and RR hold, against 2 / 2 on Do Nothing. An engine launched in 2035 would be ready too late for 2037. Press P&W and Rolls-Royce now to launch on our selection, and report the fitted sources to the Board next round.

Other moves, below the threshold and for recommendation only. The engine-slot, titanium and rare-earth agreements and the NGSA engineering recruitment should be sized to Airbus's own ramp. The Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee should confirm that none is aimed at a rival's supply chain or a rival programme's staff, so that none can be read as a bottleneck or poaching move. The Board supports the zero-for-zero trade advocacy.

Public statement: the line on funding from our own cash generation 'within our financial framework' is a capital-markets announcement reserved to the Board, and the Board accepts it as worded. Keep to windows ('the second half of the 2030s'), no payout figures, no 2040s A320 rates in our own guidance, safety first, and no reference to Delay Tactics. That window also covers a one-year slip to 2038.

Safety oversight: add to the full Board's twice-yearly safety review the NGSA ramp to 50, 80 and 100 a month, and the consolidation of the A320 14-a-month tail (about 2041-44) on the fewest lines. If the operating head reports a quality escape, a safety event or an A320neo engine crunch, the Alt plan returns to the Board, with the cash-timed view of the base plan.

Carry forward. Keep the A350 Re-engine on hold until NGSA spend rolls off. A 2035 launch overlaps NGSA in 2035-36 at $6.67B a year and fails the line, so the 2045 round is the earliest, and never after a 787 Re-engine. Delay Tactics stay off. They are to be revisited only if an fps is on the public record, and then only one poaching move under every Board condition.
