cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. The LEAP is flying on every 737 MAX and on the A320neo, and our job today is to deliver those engines on time and support that fleet. We'll keep at it with our suppliers, and with our partners at Safran.

Here's what we don't know: when the airframers will launch their next single-aisle, and what they'll want under the wing. That's really not for us to say. We don't have a birthright on that next order. So CFM will offer our engines to both airframers, and we will commit a new engine alongside a committed airframer.

RISE remains a technology programme we're all in on with Safran. The airframers will set the date for that architecture.

On the widebody, we're investing in a GEnx upgrade so the 787 fleet stays competitive for our customers.

It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
I'm placing one order: genx: upgrade_genx9. Everything else holds: ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer and lobby_emissions. RISE stays whole as technology. The narrowbody product decision comes back in 2035, once the airframers' launches and codes are on the record.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN. The game is the installed base, not share for its own sake. It is 2030 and nothing is launched: no airframe, no code, no rival NB engine, no Joint Venture commitment. This game's rules make any shift of airframe share from Boeing to Airbus cost us. Boeing loses 1 pp a year from an NGSA EIS while no fps is in service. Airbus's slack goes to Boeing, and Airbus adds 1% a year of capacity while it is short. We are sole source on the 737 and hold 60% of the A320neo. That is why hold falls to -15.23 in S2 even with CFM selected. That loss comes from the airframers, not from anything we order. Our controllables are what we put on the airframes and when.

NO BIRTHRIGHT. I read the columns where we lose the slot as hard as those where we keep it. A rival takes the whole slot in S3 (-42.50) and S6 (-60.05), and part of it in S2, S4 and S5. A Ducted does not buy back a lost slot: S3 -0.97 and S6 -4.00 against hold. It pays only where we share a new airframe with a rival: S2 +2.06 and S5 +4.44.

THE DECISION BY TEST
(1) Additive and paid for the risk. The GEnx upgrade is +0.78 in S1 and +0.77 to +0.78 in every column. It is one project, carries no strain, and GE acts alone. It is the best grid plan in S1, S3, S4 and S6, and the only order positive in all six columns.
- The Ducted fails in the expected column: S1 -4.00, its full bill. On my weights it is -0.52 against hold and -1.30 against the GEnx-alone plan it would displace, because GEnx on a Ducted alone is -1.22 once strain is netted.
- Rahul's comparator is the right one. Break-even on S2+S5 is 41% against hold, 55% against GEnx alone, and roughly 70-80% against waiting to 2035. My 40% clears none of these.
(2) Low case first. The expected column is S1 on the public record. I plan on the backlog, not on orders not yet won [CX-0248, CX-0536].
(3) Timing. The airframer sets the date. Rahul's off-grid estimate is labelled as inference. A Ducted deferred to 2035 (ready 2041) gives up about $0.49-0.72B in S2 and $0.51-0.77B in S5 against a 2030 launch. That is up to $1.13B only with a fast 7-year fps. The years lost are 2037-40, the low part of the new type's ramp.
- That is under my $1B ε, so patience wins.
- 'GEnx now, Ducted in 2035 only if S2 or S5' is worth, against hold, +0.78 / +2.24 / +0.78 / +0.77 / +4.61 / +0.77, or +1.72 weighted. A Ducted now is -0.52 and the full package -0.62.
- Caveat for 2035: if the board still counts the 2030 GEnx as running, a 2035 Ducted carries the $2B strain and pays only in S5 (+1.83). I'll ask the GM how the board treats it before the 2035 frame.
(4) H2, the Open Fan. Launched in 2030 or in 2035, it is ready in 2045 either way. Every 2030 airframe enters service first: 2037 for an NGSA or 7-year fps, 2040 for a 10-year or Embraer fps. Against hold it is -8.00 / -29.21 / -8.00 / -15.22 / -32.15 / -8.00, far beyond its $8B bill. With Lobby it is still -11.00 to -27.87. Launching now adds cost and no earlier date. I'm not spending the one RISE allowance in 2030.
(5) H3. The record holds no trigger. The grid route needs about 41% or more on S2+S5. My weights give 40% and Rahul's read of the record gives less, so a Ducted launch now is not a defence. It would be a bet on selections nobody has made.
(6) Suppliers. Ali advises one commitment per round, and Rahul's no-stacking advice agrees. Strain is the board's doctrine; Ali's supply record is my own description of his job [CX-0633].
(7) Next generation. The 20% line binds RISE. No Ducted launches, so the line stands untouched this round. If a Ducted launches in 2035, I rebut the line on physics: a ducted engine gets 'less than half' the gain [CX-0183], so it is a defensive LEAP successor and never the next generation. Durability is not traded for fuel burn [CX-0208].
(8) Tie-break. upgrade_genx9 and invest_genx are identical on the board. I take the upgrade: a derivative on a proven architecture, quality ahead of novelty.

ITEM VALUES FOR THE BOARD
- GEnx upgrade row: +0.78 / -14.46 / -41.72 / -24.25 / -35.12 / -59.28.
- Hold row: 0.00 / -15.23 / -42.50 / -25.02 / -35.90 / -60.05.

- Its value counts from 2042 unless a re-engine comes earlier (Ali). That date is the board's development time, and it is not used in public.

SAFRAN GATE (CFM parity rule)
- ducted hold: no CFM commitment, so nothing goes to Safran. The defensive Ducted comes back to the partners jointly in 2035. It is a defence that keeps a new narrowbody on CFM and serves both airframers, which is joint practice [CX-0184, CX-0185].
- open_fan hold: RISE stays the 50-50 technology programme [CX-0166, CX-0147]. No product launch is put to the partner this round.
- partner_embraer hold: it needs a new CFM engine launched, so there is nothing to put to Safran.
- lobby_emissions hold: it serves RISE and is not proposed without an Open Fan.
- genx: GE alone, no Safran gate.

HARD RULES
- H1: the LEAP derivative is offered to both airframers.
- H2: no Open Fan.
- H3: no Ducted without a trigger.
- H5: RISE is not cancelled.
- H6: no date in public.
- H7: gate stated for each order.
- H8: no rival named and no blame.
- H9: premium $0 this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game. The RISE allowance is unused.
No override is needed: neither colleague's binding test is failed by this plan.

BIASES CHECKED
- Deference to airframers can make me late to a threat. The cost of being late is measured (about $0.5-0.7B) and is under ε, and I've named the flip conditions.
- I haven't used the installed-base lens to buy a Ducted that buys nothing in S1, S3 or S6.

WHAT FLIPS ME IN 2035. A public airframer code that puts CFM on a new narrowbody alongside a rival (S2 or S5), or a rival NB engine or Joint Venture commitment on the record. Then a Ducted launches with Ali's date, the durability gate, the 20% rebuttal and a Safran sentence. If both airframers are in (S5), the Embraer partnership goes with it. In 2035 I also weigh the RISE allowance, but only on an airframer path that can wait for 2045.

Where my record is silent (Embraer, lobbying, strain), company doctrine drove the call.

On dates, every option passes his turn-on, turn-off test as the board's development times. He was candid that we have never turned a ducted product on and off: 2036 is a planning date, not a public one. I keep all dates out of the statement. His Open Fan read (2045 on either launch year, eight years after a 2037 NGSA) supports H2. His physics check matches my 20% line and the 'less than half' rebuttal I would use in 2035. No safety or durability flag is open.

I've tasked him with two things before 2035, as private moves:

- a LEAP supply review of the 9 suppliers at 15 sites.
I also need RISE ground and flight-test and compact-core durability results for any Open Fan or allowance call in 2035.

frame.question: What game are we playing, and how do we win? The game is the installed base, not share for its own sake. We want every new narrowbody on a CFM engine, and we only take risk we are paid for. "We get paid in dollars, not in percentages." It is 2030 and nothing is launched. So the question this round is narrow. Do we commit a $4B defensive Ducted now, before we know whether Airbus or Boeing launches or whom they select? Or do we take the one controllable move that pays in every column (the GEnx upgrade), keep RISE whole as technology, and decide the narrowbody in 2035 once an airframer has committed? An Open Fan product is not on the table this round. The airframer sets the date, and a 2030 Open Fan is ready in 2045, the same year as a 2035 one.

(4) Supply. You own supply, engineering and quality [CX-0633]. Does the LEAP ramp carry a Ducted, and a Ducted plus GEnx plus Embraer, without touching OE delivery? Two or more projects bring the board's $2B strain. Raw materials are our stated constraint [CX-0613]. Tell me whether to sequence one commitment per round.

BOARD GUIDANCE (labelled). The Board vetoes any launch without your ready year from test evidence set against the first new NB's EIS. It also vetoes any launch carrying a safety or durability flag that a cross-functional team has not resolved. It vetoes any 2030 Open Fan. Your record is thin after March 2024, so I will weigh your supply view against doctrine.
frame.initial_lean:
My lean is GEnx upgrade alone (genx: upgrade_genx9). It is the one controllable that pays in every column, +0.77 to +0.78, with one project and no strain. GE acts alone, so no Safran gate applies. Hold open_fan, lobby_emissions and partner_embraer. Keep RISE fully funded as technology. The RISE allowance and the Open Fan product decision belong to 2035.

The Ducted is the one live call. For now I lean to hold it.
- The public record shows no rival engine and no airframer committed. Plan on the backlog, not on the hope of orders not yet won [CX-0248, CX-0536].
- On my provisional weights (S1 .30 / S2 .25 / S3 .10 / S4 .10 / S5 .15 / S6 .10) the Ducted item is -0.52. It does not buy back the slot in S3 or S6.
- A 2035 launch keeps the option, with the airframers' codes known.
- I know my deference to airframers can make me late to a threat.

I will flip to launching the Ducted now in any of three cases: if the team's read puts more than about 40% on S2+S5; if Rahul shows a 2035 Ducted gives up more than ε in S2 and S5; or if S5 becomes my expected column. In S5, GEnx alone gives up 4.90, above the cap. That flip needs Ali's 2036 date on test evidence with no open flag. The package (D+E+G) needs about 51% on S2+S5 to pay for the strain.

Expected column: S1 on the public record, with S2 the likeliest move if anyone moves.
- In S1 the premium is 0.
- If I settle on S2 and still hold, I declare a 1.44 doctrine premium (commit a new engine with a committed airframer; one commitment per round), inside the $2.0B cap.
- I book expected PV low.

SAFRAN GATE, by narrowbody option:
- Ducted: a defence that keeps a new narrowbody on CFM and serves both airframers. That is joint practice, so consent is assumed [CX-0185, CX-0184].
- Open Fan: RISE is our 50-50 programme with Safran [CX-0166, CX-0147]. Not proposed this round.
- Partner Embraer: CFM serving every airframer [CX-0587]. Consent assumed (inference), and only with a CFM engine launched.
- Lobby: it serves RISE (inference). Not proposed without an Open Fan.

Public line in draft: we offer both airframers our engines, and CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer. RISE is all in as technology, and the airframers will set the date. No rival named, no Open Fan date before 2045, no price talk.

Safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order. It ain't that hard.

(2) Confirmed data, not early signals, puts more than about 55% on S2+S5 against the GEnx-alone plan and more than about 70-80% against waiting to 2035. cfo.memo:
Larry, the money on one page. Your item values check to the cent.

GEnx upgrade: +0.78 in S1, +0.77 in the worst column, no board R&D, one project, GE alone. Price/cost positive in every column; the only order that is.

Ducted: -4.00 in S1 and S6, its full bill. It pays only in S2 (+2.06) and S5 (+4.44), and both assume selections nobody has made. On your weights it is -0.52 against hold. The honest comparison is against GEnx alone, since GEnx cannot ride with a Ducted alone: -1.30, break-even at about 55% on S2 plus S5. We need to work the exact volume assumptions with the airframer first.

Waiting costs little. A 2035 Ducted is ready 2041; we give up the NGSA ramp years, when the A320 is still most of the line. Off grid, I estimate $0.5-0.7B in S2 and $0.5-0.9B in S5, under the $1B margin. Launching now beats waiting only above roughly 70-80% on S2 plus S5.

R&D per year: nil on GEnx, $0.67B for a Ducted, against about $2.5B. The 70% payout stays whole; no rating risk. Premium: zero in S1, 1.44 in S2; 4.90 in S5, above the cap.

What the case leaves out: S6 is -59.28, $60B below S1, and the grid assumes nobody moves again. But the good news is the GEnx stays positive even there.

Book +0.77, no upside until a launch is on the record. Plenty of work to do, and we are all over it.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (my date veto): every ready year in options A-G
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than the board's development time. Ducted at launch + 6. Open Fan at launch + 10 and not before 2045. Embraer counts at launch + 7. GEnx counts at launch + 3 and not before the first re-engine (2035 at the earliest, 2042 if none). An order whose value depends on an earlier year fails (inference: my test standard applied to the board's development times).
tests.numbers: Ducted: a 2030 launch is ready in 2036 and a 2035 launch in 2041, the years Culp's frame uses. Open Fan: a 2030 launch is ready at max(2040, 2045) = 2045, and a 2035 launch at max(2045, 2045) = 2045, as the frame says. Embraer: a 2030 launch counts from 2037. GEnx upgrade (option B): 2030 + 3 = 2033, but it counts only from the first re-engine's entry into service, which is 2042 because none is on the record (2035 at the earliest, for a re-engine launched in 2030). The grid's +0.78/+0.77 in every column (row 'GEnx upgrade' minus row 'hold everything') rests on 2042. None of options A-G depends on an earlier year. What tests stand behind the Ducted date: none on a ducted product. What we do have is RISE technology testing (over 350 tests, early focus on durability; HPT dust testing on the compact core began October 2025) and LEAP fixes delivered on test (the fuel-nozzle fix in production by March 2024; LEAP-1A HPT hardware certified December 2024). 2036 is the board's date, and I hold it as a planning date.

tests.name: Test, not analysis (my date veto): dates in the draft public line and in other moves
tests.threshold: Every date in the public statement or other moves must be one a test can back: no Open Fan entry before 2045, and no ready year before launch plus development years (hard rule 6).
tests.numbers: Culp's draft line ('we offer both airframers our engines; CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer; RISE is all in as technology; the airframers will set the date') gives no year and no Open Fan date before 2045. No other moves are proposed. Advice: keep the Ducted's 2036 and any RISE ground-test or flight-test year out of the statement. My 2022 fly-demo date ('by the middle of this decade') became 'this decade'. I will re-check the final text at the veto check.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted launched in 2030 (options C, D, E) (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. A late defensive Ducted still earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new NB is in service, so lateness does not fail it. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Ready in 2036. Against an NGSA or 7-year fps entering service in 2037 (S2, S3, S5, S6) it is 1 year ahead. Against a 10-year fps entering in 2040 (S4) it is 4 years ahead. In S1 no new NB enters service, so the +10 pp never starts and the grid shows -4.00, the bill. Margin against a 2037 NGSA is one year. On our slip record (GE9X, the RISE demo), a one-year slip still meets 2037; a two-year slip lands in 2038, one year late. Grid item against hold, S1-S6: -4.00 / +2.06 / -0.97 / -0.06 / +4.44 / -4.00.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted deferred to 2035 (option F, off grid) (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. Lateness does not fail a defensive Ducted. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Ready in 2041. Against airframes launched in 2030 it is late: 4 years after an NGSA or 7-year fps (2037) and 1 year after a 10-year fps (2040). Against airframes launched in 2035 it is early: 1 year before an NGSA or 7-year fps (2042) and 4 years before a 10-year fps (2045). Against a 2030 airframe, the years lost (2037-2040) fall in the low part of the new type's ramp: rate 50 comes about four years after entry into service, about 2041 (rules.md). What those years are worth is Ghai's estimate. If the defence is needed against a 2030 airframe, the date says launch now.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan, 2030 or 2035 launch (option G) (advice)
tests.threshold: An Open Fan ready no later than the first new narrowbody's entry into service avoids the 35 pp wait penalty (20 pp with Lobby). Report the gap. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers: Ready in 2045 on either launch year. That is 8 years after a 2037 NGSA or 7-year fps (S2, S3, S5, S6), 5 years after a 2040 10-year fps (S4), and 3 years after an NGSA launched in 2035 (2042). It is ready in time only if no NGSA or 7-year fps launches before 2038 and no 10-year or Embraer fps launches before 2035. Grid item against hold, S1-S6: -8.00 / -29.21 / -8.00 / -15.22 / -32.15 / -8.00. A 2030 launch gets no earlier year than a 2035 launch. The date itself is correct, so this is not my veto; hard rule 2 bars the launch.

tests.name: Physics (wording check)
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A ducted engine gets 'less than half' the gain, so it is never the next generation. That a Ducted is defensive only is doctrine (hard rule 3), not my words (inference).
tests.numbers: The brief has no fuel-burn data. Culp's frame says his 20% line binds RISE and that the Ducted is a defensive LEAP successor with 'less than half' the gain, never the next generation. That matches my words: 20% is 'practically impossible ... without the open fan. And the reason is physics', and a ducted engine has 'less than half the fuel burn improvements'. The draft public line calls no engine the next generation. His rebuttal of his own red line stands on physics.

tests.name: Durability first
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule. Not applicable unless the brief or a statement makes a durability claim (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers: The brief has no durability data, and no option trades durability for fuel burn or schedule. No flag is open in the record. RISE has over 350 tests with an early focus on durability, the earliest-ever HPT dust testing on its compact core, and an owner for open-fan durability. The yardstick if a Ducted launches is the LEAP gap: 9,882 cycles against about 17,000 in benign conditions, and about 4,800 against 7,000-8,000 in harsh ones, caused by a handful of parts. A Ducted's hot-and-harsh durability gate goes to a cross-functional team at launch. Confirmed for Culp: durability and fuel burn, 'the genius of the AND'; no plan here trades one for the other.

ops.memo:
We have done what we always do here: dates first, and only on test.

Open Fan. Launched in 2030 or 2035, ready in 2045. A 2030 NGSA or 7-year fps enters service in 2037, eight years earlier; a 10-year fps in 2040, five years earlier. Airframers will not wait. Hold. RISE stays whole as technology: over 350 tests, early focus on durability. I promised a fly demo by mid-decade; it became "this decade". We failed twice. We got it done.

Ducted. Launch plus six: 2036 on a 2030 launch, one year ahead of a 2037 NGSA, four ahead of a 2040 fps. Launched in 2035, ready 2041, four years late against a 2030 NGSA. 2036 passes my test as the board's development time. But precisely: we have never turned a ducted product on and turned it off. 2036 is a planning date, not a public one. It is not the next generation, and the reason is physics: less than half the gain.

No safety or durability flag is open. If the Ducted launches, hot-and-harsh durability goes to a cross-functional team. No single person can make a safety decision.

Supply: 80% of shortages came from 9 suppliers. One commitment per round; Ducted plus GEnx is -1.22 in every column. No evidence: following doctrine. On launching the Ducted, Embraer or Lobby: No evidence: following Culp.

I recommend the GEnx upgrade alone. No veto on that plan. A date before launch plus development years, or an Open Fan before 2045, I veto.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. The LEAP is flying on every 737 MAX and on the A320neo, and our job today is to deliver those engines on time and support that fleet. We'll keep at it with our suppliers, and with our partners at Safran.

Here's what we don't know: when the airframers will launch their next single-aisle, and what they'll want under the wing. That's really not for us to say. We don't have a birthright on that next order. So CFM will offer our engines to both airframers, and we will commit a new engine alongside a committed airframer.

RISE remains a technology programme we're all in on with Safran. The airframers will set the date for that architecture.

On the widebody, we're investing in a GEnx upgrade so the 787 fleet stays competitive for our customers.

It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
I'm placing one order: genx: upgrade_genx9. Everything else holds: ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer and lobby_emissions. RISE stays whole as technology. The narrowbody product decision comes back in 2035, once the airframers' launches and codes are on the record.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN. The game is the installed base, not share for its own sake. It is 2030 and nothing is launched: no airframe, no code, no rival NB engine, no Joint Venture commitment. This game's rules make any shift of airframe share from Boeing to Airbus cost us. Boeing loses 1 pp a year from an NGSA EIS while no fps is in service. Airbus's slack goes to Boeing, and Airbus adds 1% a year of capacity while it is short. We are sole source on the 737 and hold 60% of the A320neo. That is why hold falls to -15.23 in S2 even with CFM selected. That loss comes from the airframers, not from anything we order. Our controllables are what we put on the airframes and when.

NO BIRTHRIGHT. I read the columns where we lose the slot as hard as those where we keep it. A rival takes the whole slot in S3 (-42.50) and S6 (-60.05), and part of it in S2, S4 and S5. A Ducted does not buy back a lost slot: S3 -0.97 and S6 -4.00 against hold. It pays only where we share a new airframe with a rival: S2 +2.06 and S5 +4.44.

THE DECISION BY TEST
(1) Additive and paid for the risk. The GEnx upgrade is +0.78 in S1 and +0.77 to +0.78 in every column. It is one project, carries no strain, and GE acts alone. It is the best grid plan in S1, S3, S4 and S6, and the only order positive in all six columns.
- The Ducted fails in the expected column: S1 -4.00, its full bill. On my weights it is -0.52 against hold and -1.30 against the GEnx-alone plan it would displace, because GEnx on a Ducted alone is -1.22 once strain is netted.
- Rahul's comparator is the right one. Break-even on S2+S5 is 41% against hold, 55% against GEnx alone, and roughly 70-80% against waiting to 2035. My 40% clears none of these.
(2) Low case first. The expected column is S1 on the public record. I plan on the backlog, not on orders not yet won [CX-0248, CX-0536].
(3) Timing. The airframer sets the date. Rahul's off-grid estimate is labelled as inference. A Ducted deferred to 2035 (ready 2041) gives up about $0.49-0.72B in S2 and $0.51-0.77B in S5 against a 2030 launch. That is up to $1.13B only with a fast 7-year fps. The years lost are 2037-40, the low part of the new type's ramp.
- That is under my $1B ε, so patience wins.
- 'GEnx now, Ducted in 2035 only if S2 or S5' is worth, against hold, +0.78 / +2.24 / +0.78 / +0.77 / +4.61 / +0.77, or +1.72 weighted. A Ducted now is -0.52 and the full package -0.62.
- Caveat for 2035: if the board still counts the 2030 GEnx as running, a 2035 Ducted carries the $2B strain and pays only in S5 (+1.83). I'll ask the GM how the board treats it before the 2035 frame.
(4) H2, the Open Fan. Launched in 2030 or in 2035, it is ready in 2045 either way. Every 2030 airframe enters service first: 2037 for an NGSA or 7-year fps, 2040 for a 10-year or Embraer fps. Against hold it is -8.00 / -29.21 / -8.00 / -15.22 / -32.15 / -8.00, far beyond its $8B bill. With Lobby it is still -11.00 to -27.87. Launching now adds cost and no earlier date. I'm not spending the one RISE allowance in 2030.
(5) H3. The record holds no trigger. The grid route needs about 41% or more on S2+S5. My weights give 40% and Rahul's read of the record gives less, so a Ducted launch now is not a defence. It would be a bet on selections nobody has made.
(6) Suppliers. Ali advises one commitment per round, and Rahul's no-stacking advice agrees. Strain is the board's doctrine; Ali's supply record is my own description of his job [CX-0633].
(7) Next generation. The 20% line binds RISE. No Ducted launches, so the line stands untouched this round. If a Ducted launches in 2035, I rebut the line on physics: a ducted engine gets 'less than half' the gain [CX-0183], so it is a defensive LEAP successor and never the next generation. Durability is not traded for fuel burn [CX-0208].
(8) Tie-break. upgrade_genx9 and invest_genx are identical on the board. I take the upgrade: a derivative on a proven architecture, quality ahead of novelty.

ITEM VALUES FOR THE BOARD
- GEnx upgrade row: +0.78 / -14.46 / -41.72 / -24.25 / -35.12 / -59.28.
- Hold row: 0.00 / -15.23 / -42.50 / -25.02 / -35.90 / -60.05.
- Item: +0.78 / +0.77 / +0.78 / +0.77 / +0.78 / +0.77. That is +0.78 weighted on my weights or equal weights. The worst column is S6 at +0.77, bounded below.
- Its value counts from 2042 unless a re-engine comes earlier (Ali). That date is the board's development time, and it is not used in public.

SAFRAN GATE (CFM parity rule)
- ducted hold: no CFM commitment, so nothing goes to Safran. The defensive Ducted comes back to the partners jointly in 2035. It is a defence that keeps a new narrowbody on CFM and serves both airframers, which is joint practice [CX-0184, CX-0185].
- open_fan hold: RISE stays the 50-50 technology programme [CX-0166, CX-0147]. No product launch is put to the partner this round.
- partner_embraer hold: it needs a new CFM engine launched, so there is nothing to put to Safran.
- lobby_emissions hold: it serves RISE and is not proposed without an Open Fan.
- genx: GE alone, no Safran gate.

HARD RULES
- H1: the LEAP derivative is offered to both airframers.
- H2: no Open Fan.
- H3: no Ducted without a trigger.
- H5: RISE is not cancelled.
- H6: no date in public.
- H7: gate stated for each order.
- H8: no rival named and no blame.
- H9: premium $0 this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game. The RISE allowance is unused.
No override is needed: neither colleague's binding test is failed by this plan.

BIASES CHECKED
- Deference to airframers can make me late to a threat. The cost of being late is measured (about $0.5-0.7B) and is under ε, and I've named the flip conditions.
- I haven't used the installed-base lens to buy a Ducted that buys nothing in S1, S3 or S6.

WHAT FLIPS ME IN 2035. A public airframer code that puts CFM on a new narrowbody alongside a rival (S2 or S5), or a rival NB engine or Joint Venture commitment on the record. Then a Ducted launches with Ali's date, the durability gate, the 20% rebuttal and a Safran sentence. If both airframers are in (S5), the Embraer partnership goes with it. In 2035 I also weigh the RISE allowance, but only on an airframer path that can wait for 2045.

Where my record is silent (Embraer, lobbying, strain), company doctrine drove the call.

memo_weighing.ops:
Weighed for dates and the safety gate, and adopted, with the thin record noted. His own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering only. His supply view is my own description of his job [CX-0633], checked against doctrine. It agrees with the board's strain rule and with Rahul's no-stacking advice.

On dates, every option passes his turn-on, turn-off test as the board's development times. He was candid that we have never turned a ducted product on and off: 2036 is a planning date, not a public one. I keep all dates out of the statement. His Open Fan read (2045 on either launch year, eight years after a 2037 NGSA) supports H2. His physics check matches my 20% line and the 'less than half' rebuttal I would use in 2035. No safety or durability flag is open.

I've tasked him with two things before 2035, as private moves:
- a cross-functional hot-and-harsh durability gate for a Ducted;
- a LEAP supply review of the 9 suppliers at 15 sites.
I also need RISE ground and flight-test and compact-core durability results for any Open Fan or allowance call in 2035.

pratt_whitney.public_statement:
Control what you can control. The last few years on the GTF fleet were hard on our customers, and we own that. Time on wing and getting aircraft back in the air come first, ahead of any new engine.

Here is our commitment. In any round an airframer selects Pratt & Whitney for a new single-aisle, as sole source or alongside a partner, we will launch our next-generation geared turbofan that same round. It is planned to be ready six years from launch, so 2036 for a commitment made this year. Its durability will be proven before it enters service. That means time on wing ahead of fuel burn in the specification, life-limited parts at full life at entry into service, and no testing compressed to hold a date. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

We will offer it on standard terms, priced for value. We are not in the early entry phase. We are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section durability kit across the A320neo fleet, also at standard terms. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.

DECISION: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. This is Eddy's proposal and Mitchill's recommendation, and it matches my frame. Premium $0.00B. `overrides` is empty.

Team rule, step by step.
(1) Start from Eddy's proposal, row A ("GTF2 Solo if selected"): 0 / +5.59 / −19.49 / +6.37 / +9.10 / −19.49 / 0. The Board item set back to `hold` is 0 / −19.49 / −19.49 / −2.48 / −19.49 / −19.49 / 0.
(2) Strike plans that fail a binding veto. Mitchill's ground 2 (carrying an unselected engine) binds against an unconditional `launch` (rows C and E). His ground 4 (booking upside before it is proven) binds against any `jv_with_rr: commit` (rows D and E, and hold plus commit). I accept both. Neither is on a ground I would contest, and the rule gives me no override. Eddy raises no binding veto on any row. Row A passes all six ExCo grounds.
(3) Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073]. A 2030 trigger is ready in 2036. That is one year inside a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-yr EIS, and four years inside a 2040 fps 10-yr or Embraer EIS. Eddy's binding check passes. I note my own bias here: my operating dates have slipped by a quarter to about two years [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104], and Eddy's slip prior is +1.5 to 2 years. So I do not lean on the one-year margin. I write in his conditions: time on wing and LLP life ahead of fuel burn, severe-environment endurance testing before certification, full-life parts at EIS, a weekly drumbeat on maturity gates, and no compressed testing. The public statement says "planned", not a promise.
(4) Optimise inside the constraint. On my weights, expected ΔPV is: A −2.49 (+7.51 against hold); C −3.12; C with the 2035 cancel −2.99; D −2.69; hold −9.99. A is the best row on my weights, on Mitchill's (A −4.24, +5.63 against hold) and on equal weights (+8.93). It is also never below hold in any column, so it clears the return hurdle on any weights.
(5) Visible-demand test [PX-0109][PX-0009]. `launch_if_selected` spends only if a live airframe selects a code with P&W (2, 6 or 7) this round. The commitment arrives with the demand. The edge of `launch` over `launch_if_selected` is 0.37·p(S3) + 1.14·p(S6) − 2.00·[p(S1)+p(S7)]. On my weights that is −0.63 (−0.50 with the 2035 cancel at $1.67B); Mitchill gets −0.67 (−0.53) and equal weights give −0.36. Break-even needs 64% on S6 against S1 plus S7, and the Board needs 80%. The hedge fails, and no premium can buy it.
(6) Miss-a-cycle test [PX-0071]. That line was said of RTX's businesses in general, so applying it to GTF2 is inference. Any column where NGSA enters service without us costs −19.49, about 18% of EV. This round is the only one that can serve an airframe launched in 2030: a GTF2 launched in 2035 is ready in 2041, too late. `launch_if_selected` answers that test at zero cost unless we are selected. The S3 and S6 losses come from Airbus's selection, not from our order. An unconditional launch only moves them to −19.12 and −18.35. We answer that with product, not price [PX-0055].
(7) Joint Venture: `hold`. Rolls-Royce has no commitment on the public record, and no live airframe has a code that includes Rolls-Royce. A commit is worth 0 in S1 to S6 and −2.00 in S7. My record is silent here, so this is doctrine [P-1233] plus Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test, as my fallback requires.
(8) Dividend and debt [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669]. A triggered GTF2 is about $0.33B a year from 2030 to 2035, or 5.6% of the roughly $6B self-funded envelope, even in S5. Mitchill confirms the dividend stays covered and the pre-ASR debt path is untouched.
(9) Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]. There is no discount, concession or free upgrade in other moves or in the statement. The kit is sold at standard terms.

Doctrine relief, declared at $0. A shared-source trigger (codes 6 or 7) is accepted against the sole-source red line [P-0746]. On NGSA it is also franchise defence: we aimed at about 40% of the shared A320neo [PX-0058][P-1292]. That is inference.

Not booked. Three things are excluded from every number above:
- the S3 code switch (Airbus moving NGSA to a P&W code in 2035, where only a GTF2 launched in 2030 would be ready by 2037);
- any Rolls-Royce commitment or 2035 Joint Venture fold-in (Eddy's door through a Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB solo launched in 2030 has zero margin and is Rolls-Royce's architecture);
- any durability gain from the kit.

Booked number in S1: $0.00B.

Round 2 contingencies, written in now:

A GTF2 launched in 2035 would be ready in 2041, after a 2037 NGSA EIS, and an NGSA in service without P&W costs us -19.49.

2. Return hurdle and proof before commitment. No unconditional `launch` into an empty public record. Against `launch_if_selected` it adds only +0.37 in S3 and +1.14 in S6, and it loses -2.00 in S1 and S7. That falls short of the Board's +$0.5B franchise-defence margin on any plausible weights.

3. Keep the Joint Venture at `hold` this round. A `commit` is worth 0 in every column except S7, where it costs -2.00. Rolls-Royce has made no commitment on the public record, and no live airframe has a code that includes Rolls-Royce. If a Joint Venture does come, it shares risk and never the gear.

4. Durability and the fleet first. A GTF2 launched in 2030 is ready in 2036. That is in time for an NGSA or fps 7-yr EIS in 2037, and for an fps 10-yr or Embraer EIS in 2040. GTF fleet recovery and parts supply must not be drawn down to pay for it.
5. Keep the dividend and the debt path whole. A triggered GTF2 costs about $0.33B a year (about 5-6% of the ~$6B self-funded envelope), so no stretch is needed.
board_guidance.risk_appetite: 3.5 this round: the Board is strict on programme commitments and relaxed about conditional ones. We will approve `launch_if_selected` readily. We will not approve an unconditional GTF2 launch or a Joint Venture commit while the public record shows no selection and no Rolls-Royce commitment. The balance sheet is not strained: at most about $0.33B a year of new R&D, and only if a selection triggers it.
board_guidance.expect_to_see: The Board expects the following in the package. (1) The grid row of the submitted orders, and the row with each Board item set back to `hold`. If the package is `launch_if_selected` with `jv_with_rr` at `hold`, those rows are 0 / +5.59 / -19.49 / +6.37 / +9.10 / -19.49 / 0 against 0 / -19.49 / -19.49 / -2.48 / -19.49 / -19.49 / 0. (2) The CEO's expected scenario, his `predictions` over S1-S7, and `premium_b`; we expect 0, because `launch_if_selected` needs no premium. (3) Mitchill's column probabilities, his expected item value against `hold`, and, if an unconditional `launch` is proposed, his expected edge over `launch_if_selected`, computed as 0.37·p(S3) + 1.14·p(S6) − 2.00·[p(S1)+p(S7)]. He should also show the named cancel round (2035, write-off $1.67B; GTF2 is ready in 2036 and can only be cancelled before then) and the envelope check (about $0.33B a year inside about $6B). (4) Eddy's ready year (2036 for a 2030 launch) set against every EIS a rival could reach from a 2030 launch (2037 for NGSA or fps 7-yr, 2040 for fps 10-yr or Embraer), plus his parts and capacity result for the GTF fleet. (5) Both ExCo veto checks: Mitchill's four grounds and Eddy's two, with nothing overridden. (6) The draft public statement and any `other_moves`, with whether each is public. If any piece is missing, the Board will compute it from the brief and say so; a missing piece is not on its own a ground for veto.
would_approve: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`. Its value against `hold` is S1 0, S2 +25.08, S3 0, S4 +8.85, S5 +28.59, S6 0, S7 0. That is at least 0 in every column, so it clears the return hurdle on any weights. Its downside is bounded, since nothing is spent unless the order triggers. Its value in S2, S4 and S5 depends on its own trigger (a selection), not on upside booked in advance. It is ready by 2036, before any EIS reachable from a 2030 launch, and it fits the envelope at about $0.33B a year. This is the form the Board's doctrine prefers [P-0746, P-0737, P-1347].

`gtf2_solo: launch` only if Mitchill's weights give an edge over `launch_if_selected` of at least +$0.5B, i.e. 0.37·p(S3) + 1.14·p(S6) − 2.00·[p(S1)+p(S7)] ≥ 0.5. It must also name 2035 as its cancel round (write-off $1.67B) and keep the dividend whole. In practice this needs about 80% odds on S6 against S1 and S7, and at most 20.4% combined weight on S1 and S7 even if every other point of weight sits on S6. S3 alone (+0.37) can never carry it.
`hold` on either field. This is not a Board item and is never vetoed, but the Board recommends against `gtf2_solo: hold` this round (see Miss a cycle).

`jv_with_rr: commit` in a later round, once Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the public record or a live airframe not yet in service has a code that includes Rolls-Royce (1, 4, 5 or 7), and its weighted item value is at least 0, or falls short by no more than a declared premium of up to $0.5B.
would_veto: `gtf2_solo: launch` (unconditional) in round 1, on any weights that give less than +$0.5B edge over `launch_if_selected`. No selection is on the public record, so the Committed airframe test (a) cannot be met. Test (b), franchise defence, fails because the launch adds only +0.37 in S3 and +1.14 in S6 and loses -2.00 in S1 and S7. On equal weights the edge is -0.36. Grounds: uncommitted airframe and return hurdle [P-0731, P-0746, P-0737, P-1367]. Acceptable alternatives: `launch_if_selected`, `hold`.

`jv_with_rr: commit` in round 1. It fails the Joint Venture test: Rolls-Royce has no commitment on the public record and no live airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7. Its item value is 0 in S1-S6 and -2.00 in S7, so it can only be negative. A declared premium cannot rescue it, because with no live airframe it does not serve the objective. Grounds: Joint Venture conditions and return hurdle [P-1233, P-1875, PG-0047]. Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

Any engine item whose case rests on unrecorded upside, for example an assumed code change by Airbus in 2035 or an assumed Rolls-Royce commitment. The grid assumes nobody moves after this round. Ground: unproven upside [P-1367, PX-0311, PX-0350].
Any item carrying an unresolved veto from Mitchill or Eddy, an unrebutted red-line flag, or any entry in `overrides`. Ground: governance [P-1285, PX-0199, PG-0016].
Any engine item that Eddy fails on durability or parts, unless his veto check shows the problem resolved. Ground: durability [P-1360, P-1215, PG-0050].

recommendations.text: Miss a cycle: order `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected` this round. If every order is `hold`, the round never reaches the Board, and an NGSA launched in 2030 without P&W is lost for good. A GTF2 launched in 2035 would be ready in 2041, after a 2037 EIS. `launch_if_selected` costs nothing unless an airframer selects a code with P&W (2, 6 or 7). If one does, it turns -19.49 into +5.59 (S2), -2.48 into +6.37 (S4) and -19.49 into +9.10 (S5).

Show the return against Do Nothing and against a buyback. Present the submitted row beside the `hold` row, Mitchill's weights over S1-S7, and the weighted item value. On equal weights, `launch_if_selected` is worth about +8.93 against `hold`, and an unconditional `launch` is worth about 0.36 less than `launch_if_selected`. At a 10% discount rate, a positive item value clears the hurdle the Board was given.

Keep `jv_with_rr` at `hold`. Revisit in 2035 if Rolls-Royce commits publicly or a live fps or NGSA code includes Rolls-Royce (1, 4, 5 or 7). If the Joint Venture forms, it shares risk and investment, never the gear or core technology. Note that a commitment is public the moment it is made.

Public statement: state the conditional offer plainly. GTF2 launches in the round an airframer selects P&W and is ready six years after launch (2036 for a 2030 launch). Promise no earlier EIS, no durability not yet proven, nothing about an airframer's dates, and no selection or Rolls-Royce commitment that is not on the record.

Durability and the fleet first. Eddy should confirm that a triggered GTF2 does not draw engineering or parts away from GTF fleet recovery, and that time on wing comes before fuel burn in its specification. The fleet beats a new engine.

Dividend and debt path. Mitchill should confirm that a triggered GTF2 (about $0.33B a year, about 5-6% of the ~$6B self-funded R&D and capex envelope) leaves the dividend covered and debt on its pre-ASR path. No envelope stretch is needed or asked for.

Other moves: no launch-style pricing or deep discount to buy an NGSA selection. A rival's discount never moves the answer. Fleet-facing moves that are public and that P&W has historically made, such as the GTF Advantage durability kit across the A320neo fleet, are welcome. They change no payoff.

frame.question: Control what you can control [PX-0020]. We do not control whether Airbus launches NGSA or Boeing launches fps this year, or which engine either of them names. We do control two things. First, whether P&W is still in the running when they choose. Second, what we promise the market about durability. The question this round: what order on `gtf2_solo` and `jv_with_rr` keeps us in the running for any new narrowbody launched in 2030, with no capital spent ahead of visible demand, the dividend and debt path untouched, and nothing promised that we have not yet proven? Round 1 is our only chance at a 2030-launched airframe. A GTF2 launched in 2035 is ready in 2041, after a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-yr EIS and after a 2040 fps 10-yr or Embraer EIS. If we miss this cycle, we are shut out of it for decades [PX-0071][P-1347]. That line was said of RTX's businesses in general, so applying it to GTF2 is inference.
frame.situation: Public record, 2030: no programme launched, no engine selected, and no Rolls-Royce Joint Venture commitment. Everyone is on today's products. Airbus is on its base A320 plan (85 a month until NGSA, then the lines wind down). Boeing's fps would be built at new sites. Observed 2026-29: P&W holds 24.2% of narrowbody engines, which is our 40% of the A320neo slot. This run's assumptions are in rules.md: the conservative demand case (1,406 aircraft in 2030, peaking at 2,019 in 2045), with the firm backlog lasting to about 2035; Boeing loses 1 pp a year from NGSA EIS while no fps is in service; Airbus slack goes to Boeing; Airbus adds 1% of capacity a year whenever it is short. The bad news first. Our status quo is ΔPV −0.00 (yield 100.0%). Neither objective test is met: no new P&W engine on a new airframe (credibility), and ΔPV is not above zero (capitalise). On the grid, every column in which NGSA enters service without P&W costs us −19.49, about 18% of our $110B EV, as NGSA replaces the A320neo slot. An fps 10-yr in service without us costs −2.48 (S4 on hold). `launch_if_selected` turns S2 into +5.59, S4 into +6.37 and S5 into +9.10. It is never below `hold` in any column (+25.08 / +8.85 / +28.59 in S2 / S4 / S5, 0 elsewhere). S3 and S6, where NGSA launches without us, stay at about −19 whatever we order. An unconditional launch only moves them to −19.12 and −18.35. That loss comes from the selection, not from our order, and we answer it with product, not price [PX-0055]. Readiness: a 2030 GTF2 is ready in 2036. That is one year inside a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-yr EIS, and four years inside a 2040 fps 10-yr or Embraer EIS. My own operating dates have slipped before, by a quarter to about two years [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104], so a one-year margin needs Eddy's check, not my optimism. Board guidance: it approves `launch_if_selected` readily. It would veto an unconditional `launch` unless the expected edge over `launch_if_selected` is at least +$0.5B, would veto a `jv_with_rr: commit` this round, and would veto any case resting on unrecorded upside.
levers_in_play: `gtf2_solo`: `hold` | `launch` | `launch_if_selected` ($2B R&D, about $0.33B a year; ready 6 years after launch, so 2036 for a 2030 launch; a 2030 launch can be cancelled only in 2035, write-off $1.67B)

`jv_with_rr`: `hold` | `commit` (public at once and standing until withdrawn; $2B P&W share; the Joint Venture forms when Rolls-Royce also commits and is ready 6 years after formation, earlier if a solo programme that is further along folds in; a live GTF2 folds in and its spend counts toward our $2B)
Not on the grid: `other_moves` (public or not) and the `public_statement`. Durability kit, standard terms, the conditional offer. None of them changes a payoff.
options_to_test: A. `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold`: 0 / +5.59 / −19.49 / +6.37 / +9.10 / −19.49 / 0. My lean. Against `hold`: 0 / +25.08 / 0 / +8.85 / +28.59 / 0 / 0, never negative.
B. `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold` (Do Nothing; the Board's reference row): 0 / −19.49 / −19.49 / −2.48 / −19.49 / −19.49 / 0. Test it as the miss-a-cycle baseline, not as a candidate.

C. `gtf2_solo: launch`, `jv_with_rr: hold` (the NGSA franchise hedge): −2.00 / +5.59 / −19.12 / +6.37 / +9.10 / −18.35 / −2.00. Minus A by column: −2.00 / 0 / +0.37 / 0 / 0 / +1.14 / −2.00. Edge = 0.37·p(S3) + 1.14·p(S6) − 2.00·[p(S1)+p(S7)]. Also show it with the 2035 cancel written in (−1.67 instead of −2.00 in S1 and S7). On equal weights the edge is about −0.36; on my early weights it is about −0.63 (−0.50 with the cancel). It passes only if Mitchill's edge is ≥ 0, and the Board needs ≥ +0.5.

D. `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: commit`: 0 / +5.59 / −19.49 / +6.37 / +9.10 / −19.49 / −2.00. The Joint Venture's own cost is −2.00 in S7 and nothing in any other column. It isolates the Joint Venture: off by my default, since Rolls-Royce is not on the record and no live airframe has a code with Rolls-Royce in it.

E. `gtf2_solo: launch`, `jv_with_rr: commit`: identical to C in every column, because a live GTF2 folds in. Test it only to confirm the fold-in arithmetic. It still fails the Joint Venture conditions this round.
Dominated, not worth testing: `hold` plus `commit` (−2.00 in S7, no better anywhere).
red_lines: Safety and durability first [PX-0035][PX-0073]. No P&W engine goes on an airframe before it is ready and its durability is proven before EIS. GTF2 (2036 for a 2030 launch) or the Joint Venture engine must be ready by the selecting airframe's EIS. Eddy's readiness and durability check binds me.
The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]. A triggered GTF2 must not draw engineering, parts or MRO capacity away from GTF fleet recovery and bending the AOG curve. Eddy's parts and capacity veto binds.

No new engine without a committed airframer [P-0746]: on this board that means `launch_if_selected`. An unconditional `launch` is allowed only into a P&W selection already on the public record (there is none), or as the NGSA franchise hedge with Mitchill's expected edge over `launch_if_selected` ≥ 0 (his ground 2 binds; no premium buys it) and the Board's ≥ +$0.5B. It needs a named 2035 cancel. No hedge for fps alone, and never a launch for share alone.

Sole source: a shared-source trigger (codes 6 or 7) is accepted and declared as doctrine relief. On NGSA it is also franchise defence; we aimed at about 40% of the shared A320neo [PX-0058][P-1292]. This is inference.

Joint Venture [P-1233]: share risk and investment, never the gear or our core technology. A commitment is public at once. It is off unless Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the public record or a live airframe's code includes Rolls-Royce (1, 4, 5 or 7). Neither holds in 2030.
Dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669]. No plan that needs a dividend cut or reverses the debt path. Mitchill confirms.
Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]: no launch-style discount, concession or free upgrade in other moves or in the statement to win a selection. A rival's discount never moves the answer.
Narrowbody only [PX-0027]. We have no widebody move.
We never speak for an airframer's dates or rates [PX-0062], and never claim a selection or a Rolls-Royce commitment that is not on the record.
One premium cap: doctrine plus objective premium ≤ $1B (objectives.md §6). The Board passes an item that trails `hold` only on a declared premium of ≤ $0.5B that serves the objective.

Board's would-veto list, carried in: an unconditional `launch` with edge < +$0.5B; `jv_with_rr: commit` in round 1; any item resting on unrecorded upside (an assumed Airbus code change in 2035, an assumed Rolls-Royce commitment); any item with an unresolved Mitchill or Eddy veto, an unrebutted red-line flag, or an entry in `overrides` (we leave `overrides` empty); any item Eddy fails on durability or parts; any item that can lose more than its own $2B against `hold` in a plausible column.
frame.asks_cfo:
Neil, I trust your cash numbers over my operating dates. Please give me the following.
(1) Your probabilities over S1-S7. Then each row's expected PV and worst column for rows A to E, with `hold` beside them, as the Board asked.
(2) The `launch` minus `launch_if_selected` difference by column (−2.00 / 0 / +0.37 / 0 / 0 / +1.14 / −2.00) and its expected edge on your weights, with and without the 2035 cancel written in (write-off $1.67B in place of the full $2.00B in S1 and S7). State the break-even mix: the S6 weight against S1 plus S7 at which the edge reaches 0, and where it reaches the Board's +0.5. Rule on ground 2 (carrying an unselected engine). Your ground binds, and I will not buy a hedge that fails it with a premium.
(3) The Joint Venture: confirm its cost if Rolls-Royce commits and nobody selects it (−2.00 in S7). Confirm that net of a live GTF2 it adds nothing, because the GTF2 spend folds into our $2B share (row E equals row C).
(4) Cancel: confirm 2035 is the only cancel round for a 2030 launch (ready 2036), with a $1.67B write-off. Confirm that a triggered `launch_if_selected` is never cancelled while the airframe that selected us is live.
(5) Dividend and debt: a triggered GTF2 is about $0.33B a year. Show it inside the roughly $10B of E&D and capex, about $6B of it self-funded. Confirm the dividend stays covered and the pre-ASR debt path is not reversed in any column, including S5, where both selections land on us.
(6) Your ruling on all four grounds for each candidate row: dividend and debt, unselected engine, aggressive terms (applies to other moves only on this board), booked upside.
(7) Mark what we must not book. The main item: in S3, Airbus could switch NGSA's code to include P&W in 2035, and only a GTF2 launched in 2030 would be ready by 2037. That is real option value, but the grid assumes nobody moves after this round. Name it, do not count it.
frame.asks_ops:
Shane, your proposal leads. Please give me the following.
(1) Your engine-order proposal on `gtf2_solo` and `jv_with_rr`, with the reasoning.
(2) Readiness: a GTF2 launched in 2030 is ready in 2036. Set that against every EIS a rival can reach from a 2030 launch: NGSA 2037, fps 7-yr 2037, fps 10-yr or Embraer 2040. The NGSA margin is one year, and I have missed dates by a quarter to two years before [PX-0017][PX-0098]. Is six years credible, with durability proven (time on wing before fuel burn in the spec, test hours and maturity gates) before a 2037 EIS? We learned that lesson on prior GTF iterations [PX-0073].
(3) Joint Venture readiness with fold-in. If both commit in 2030, it is ready in 2036. If it forms in 2035, it is ready in 2041, unless a further-along solo programme folds in: a live GTF2, or a Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB solo launched in 2030 and ready in 2037. In the S3 and S6 columns, NGSA carries Rolls-Royce on code 5. Tell me whether a 2035 Joint Venture could still meet a 2037 EIS, and what it would cost in engineering. I am not booking it. I want to know whether the door exists for round 2.
(4) Pacing parts and capacity for the GTF fleet: AOG trend, hot-section parts, MRO slots. Confirm that a triggered GTF2 does not draw engineering or parts away from fleet recovery. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].
(5) The engineering load of the plan if one or both selections trigger (S5), against our engineering-resources constraint.
(6) Your ruling on your two veto grounds for each candidate row: durability not proven before EIS, and parts or capacity short of the fleet's needs.
(7) Whether you want the GTF Advantage durability kit across the A320neo fleet as a public other move. It is charged at standard terms, not given away [PX-0100][PX-0088][PX-0106].
frame.initial_lean:
My lean is A: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected` and `jv_with_rr: hold`, with premium $0B. It never trails `hold` in any column, and it is the best grid plan on any weights I find plausible. On my early sketch (S1 .30, S2 .15, S3 .15, S4 .10, S5 .10, S6 .10, S7 .10) it is worth about +7.5 against `hold`; on equal weights about +8.9. It answers visible demand in the round it appears [PX-0109][PX-0009]. It is the only form that serves the assigned objective without spending ahead of a selection: in S2, S4 and S5 it meets both credibility (GTF2 in service on NGSA in 2037 or fps in 2040, before 2050) and capitalise (ΔPV > 0). A shared-source trigger (codes 6 or 7) is accepted and declared as doctrine relief, not a premium.

My bias is to see the next single-aisle "mid-next decade" [PX-0093]. That is exactly why I will not sit on `hold` and miss a 2030 selection. The unconditional `launch` hedge stays on the table only if Neil's weights give it an edge of at least 0 (and the Board's +0.5). On my own sketch it is about −0.63, or −0.50 with the 2035 cancel, so I expect it to fail. The S3 code-switch option is real but unrecorded, and I will not book it. The Joint Venture stays at `hold`: no Rolls-Royce commitment on the record, and no live code with Rolls-Royce in it. I revisit it in 2035 if either changes, with the gear never on the table [P-1233][PX-0014]. I will adjust on Neil's numbers and Shane's readiness check, not on any rival's price.

Proposed disclosure (public statement): "The GTF fleet is not where it needs to be, and we own that. Time on wing and getting aircraft back in the air come first. Pratt & Whitney will commit its next-generation geared turbofan in any round an airframer selects us, as sole source or alongside a partner. It is ready six years from launch, 2036 for a commitment this year, and its durability will be proven before it enters service. We will offer it on standard terms, priced for value. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. We will not get ahead of any airframer's own plans."

Proposed other move (public, no payoff effect): continue the GTF Advantage hot-section durability kit across the A320neo fleet at standard terms. No launch-style pricing, no free upgrade.

cfo.memo:
Low end first. On my weights (S1 .35, S2 .15, S3 .15, S4 .05, S5 .05, S6 .15, S7 .10), Do Nothing is worth −9.87, with −19.49 in four columns. My first read was timing: nothing hits before a 2037 NGSA EIS. It's more pervasive than that. NGSA takes the A320neo slot, and our order doesn't change whom Airbus picks.

`launch_if_selected` is the plan. It's worth −4.24, +5.63 against hold, and it's never below hold in any column. It spends nothing unless an airframer selects us. If it triggers, it costs about $0.33B a year in 2030-35, about 5-6% of a $6B self-funded envelope, even in S5. The V2500 and GTF aftermarket fund the bridge. The dividend stays covered and the debt path to pre-ASR levels is untouched. We do not want to starve the business, and this doesn't.

An unconditional `launch` fails my gate. Against `launch_if_selected` it's −2.00 / 0 / +0.37 / 0 / 0 / +1.14 / −2.00. The edge is −0.67 on my weights, −0.53 with a 2035 cancel and its $1.67B write-off. Break-even is 64% S6 against S1 plus S7; the Board's +0.5 needs 80%. Veto, ground 2, binding.

Joint Venture: hold. Rolls-Royce isn't on the record. It's 0, or −2.00 in S7, and a live GTF2 folds in at no new cost (E equals C).

Booked number: 0.00 in S1. The S3 code-switch is real option value; we name it, we don't count it. I'd like to see a few more reps first.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ORDERS: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold` (Calio's row A). Grid row "GTF2 Solo if selected": 0 / +5.59 / -19.49 / +6.37 / +9.10 / -19.49 / 0, against `hold` at 0 / -19.49 / -19.49 / -2.48 / -19.49 / -19.49 / 0. That is never below `hold`.

WHY `launch_if_selected`. An NGSA launched this year and in service in 2037 without us costs -19.49. A GTF2 launched in 2035 is ready in 2041, after every EIS reachable from a 2030 launch, so this is the cycle. The order ties the launch to a customer, keeps engineering on the fleet until one shows up, and can only trigger if GTF2 would be ready by that airframe's EIS (rules.md). This is the seat's doctrine (GTF2 only into a selection, with the durability programme intact), not my own record, which has no launch decision in it.

WHY `jv_with_rr: hold`. Rolls-Royce's commitment is not on the record, no live airframe has code 1, 4, 5 or 7, and nothing on the board protects our gear and core [P-1233].

ANSWERS TO CALIO
(1) As above.
(2) Readiness. Launch 2030, ready 2036. NGSA EIS 2037 and fps 7-yr EIS 2037: one year of margin. fps 10-yr and Embraer EIS 2040: four years. That passes the binding test. One year is my advisory minimum and nothing more: my Advantage certification went from mid-2024 to 2025, and the company's derivative slip prior is +1.5 to 2 years. Six years is credible only if: time on wing and LLP life come ahead of fuel burn in the spec [PX-0073]; severe-environment endurance testing is done before certification, because 3/4 of the fleet flew cool and hid the hot-and-sandy shortfall [PX-0122], and the Advantage needed more than double the endurance testing [P-0779]; all LLPs are at full life at EIS [PX-0128]; and maturity gates are reviewed on the weekly drumbeat [PX-0131]. If test data in 2035 put 2036 at risk, you get the bad number first. We never compress testing to hold the date.
(3) Joint Venture with fold-in. If both commit in 2030 it is ready in 2036. If it forms in 2035 it is ready in 2041, unless a solo programme folds in. A live GTF2 makes it 2036, but only after an unconditional launch: `launch_if_selected` leaves no GTF2 in S3 or S6. An RR UltraFan NB launched in 2030 makes it 2037, with zero margin. So the door to a 2037 NGSA exists on the board's arithmetic, but only through RR's 2030 solo, and only if Airbus moves NGSA's code to 4 or 7 in 2035, which is unrecorded and not booked. It is narrow. Zero margin fails my advisory margin. We would be signing durability on an engine we did not design or test, two years from service, built on RR's architecture, not an extended GTF. Cost: our $2B share. I would not go through that door without RR's severe-environment test data.
(4) Parts. The 2030 brief and bulletin show no live fleet, quality or supply problem, so ground 2 passes. The board does not model parts. My last numbers are from June 2023: 10% of the fleet AOG, about 30 pacing parts, shops waiting on parts rather than capacity, castings +40%, 60% of the fleet in the latest configuration. The CFO projected about 350 AOG through 2026 [PX-0300]. The AOG trend, hot-section parts and MRO slots for 2030 are not in my evidence, and I will not invent them. Development to 2036 draws engineers and test hardware, not production castings. The squeeze is the GTF2 production ramp from 2036 alongside NGSA's: the powder-metal escape came from a ramp [P-1040]. Condition (inference): fleet spares rank ahead of GTF2 installs on the pacing-parts list.
(5) Engineering load in S5: one development ($2B, about $0.33B a year from 2030 to 2036) and two installs, NGSA in 2037 plus fps in 2040, or both in 2037 if the fps is a 7-yr. No second programme while the Joint Venture is at `hold`. There is no strain charge on the board, so this is advice and it passes.
(6) Veto rulings. Row A: passes both grounds. Row B: passes both, though it misses the cycle (not my ground). Rows C and E: pass both grounds (ready 2036, no live problem), so no binding veto, but I do not propose them because the engine would have no customer. Row D: passes both grounds, but the Joint Venture conditions fail. No binding veto on any row.
(7) The kit: yes, as a public other move at standard terms, pass-through pricing and no free upgrade [PX-0100][PX-0117]. Report the percentage of the fleet in the latest configuration [PX-0116], not a dated AOG recovery, because my dated recoveries slipped [PX-0115]. The kit's hot-section parts are themselves pacing parts, so fleet first.

ops.would_change_mind_if: I would change my view on any of the following. (1) Severe-environment test data, or a test plan, showing GTF2 durability cannot be proven by 2036. Then I would reopen readiness against a 2037 EIS on ground 1 and keep the 2040 case. (2) A brief or bulletin that shows a live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem: rising AOG, an escape, a durability crisis. Then I contain first with a dated recovery, and any unconditional launch fails ground 2. (3) A P&W selection on the public record. Then I would propose `launch` into it, with readiness passed. (4) Rolls-Royce's commitment on the record, or a live code with Rolls-Royce (1, 4, 5 or 7). Then I would state the Joint Venture's technical conditions (ready by EIS with any fold-in; our gear and core stay ours) and leave the call to Calio. ops.memo:
The bad number first: an NGSA in service in 2037 without us costs $19.49B, our 40% of the A320neo slot. A GTF2 launched in 2035 is ready in 2041, too late for any airframe launched this year.

I propose `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. Triggered in 2030, GTF2 is ready in 2036: one year inside a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-yr EIS, four inside a 2040 fps 10-yr or Embraer. One year is my minimum, not a cushion: my Advantage certification went from mid-2024 to 2025. So no EIS promise before launch plus six, all life-limited parts at full life at entry into service, time on wing ahead of fuel burn, and no compressed testing to hold a date. If the 2035 test data say 2036 is slipping, you hear it from me first.

Parts: the brief shows no live fleet, quality or supply problem, so ground 2 passes; the board does not model parts. Development draws engineers, not castings. The squeeze comes with the production ramp from 2036, and fleet spares stay ahead of new installs.

No binding veto on any row. I do not propose an unconditional launch: no customer. The Joint Venture stays at hold: Rolls-Royce is not on the record, and our gear is not on the table.

The kit: yes, public, standard terms, reported by configuration percentage, not a dated AOG promise.

My record is one event, June 2023, before the recall. Where it is silent, this is the seat's doctrine.

other_moves.move: GTF Advantage hot-section durability kit across the A320neo fleet
other_moves.detail: We keep fitting the hot-section durability kit across the in-service A320neo GTF fleet. It is sold at standard terms with pass-through pricing: no free upgrade and no launch-style discount [PX-0100][PX-0088][PX-0106]. We report progress as the percentage of the fleet in the latest configuration, not as a dated AOG recovery (Eddy's advice; my own dated recoveries have slipped) [PX-0098][PX-0104]. It changes no payoff on the board.

other_moves.move: Fleet-first priority on pacing parts
other_moves.detail: This is an internal rule and is not published. If GTF2 triggers, GTF fleet spares and MRO material rank ahead of GTF2 production installs on the pacing-parts list from the 2036 ramp onward. Development to 2036 draws engineers and test hardware, not production castings. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]. Eddy's condition is adopted as written.

other_moves.move: 2035 review gates written into the plan
other_moves.detail: This is internal. If GTF2 has triggered, Eddy reports severe-environment endurance test data and maturity gates against the 2036 ready date before the 2035 round, and the bad number comes first. We do not compress testing to hold the date. On the Joint Venture, we revisit only if Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the public record or a live airframe's code includes Rolls-Royce (1, 4, 5 or 7). The gear and core technology are never on the table [P-1233].

decision.public_statement:
Control what you can control. The last few years on the GTF fleet were hard on our customers, and we own that. Time on wing and getting aircraft back in the air come first, ahead of any new engine.

Here is our commitment. In any round an airframer selects Pratt & Whitney for a new single-aisle, as sole source or alongside a partner, we will launch our next-generation geared turbofan that same round. It is planned to be ready six years from launch, so 2036 for a commitment made this year. Its durability will be proven before it enters service. That means time on wing ahead of fuel burn in the specification, life-limited parts at full life at entry into service, and no testing compressed to hold a date. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF.

We will offer it on standard terms, priced for value. We are not in the early entry phase. We are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section durability kit across the A320neo fleet, also at standard terms. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. This is Eddy's proposal and Mitchill's recommendation, and it matches my frame. Premium $0.00B. `overrides` is empty.

Team rule, step by step.
(1) Start from Eddy's proposal, row A ("GTF2 Solo if selected"): 0 / +5.59 / −19.49 / +6.37 / +9.10 / −19.49 / 0. The Board item set back to `hold` is 0 / −19.49 / −19.49 / −2.48 / −19.49 / −19.49 / 0.
(2) Strike plans that fail a binding veto. Mitchill's ground 2 (carrying an unselected engine) binds against an unconditional `launch` (rows C and E). His ground 4 (booking upside before it is proven) binds against any `jv_with_rr: commit` (rows D and E, and hold plus commit). I accept both. Neither is on a ground I would contest, and the rule gives me no override. Eddy raises no binding veto on any row. Row A passes all six ExCo grounds.
(3) Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073]. A 2030 trigger is ready in 2036. That is one year inside a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-yr EIS, and four years inside a 2040 fps 10-yr or Embraer EIS. Eddy's binding check passes. I note my own bias here: my operating dates have slipped by a quarter to about two years [PX-0017][PX-0098][PX-0104], and Eddy's slip prior is +1.5 to 2 years. So I do not lean on the one-year margin. I write in his conditions: time on wing and LLP life ahead of fuel burn, severe-environment endurance testing before certification, full-life parts at EIS, a weekly drumbeat on maturity gates, and no compressed testing. The public statement says "planned", not a promise.
(4) Optimise inside the constraint. On my weights, expected ΔPV is: A −2.49 (+7.51 against hold); C −3.12; C with the 2035 cancel −2.99; D −2.69; hold −9.99. A is the best row on my weights, on Mitchill's (A −4.24, +5.63 against hold) and on equal weights (+8.93). It is also never below hold in any column, so it clears the return hurdle on any weights.
(5) Visible-demand test [PX-0109][PX-0009]. `launch_if_selected` spends only if a live airframe selects a code with P&W (2, 6 or 7) this round. The commitment arrives with the demand. The edge of `launch` over `launch_if_selected` is 0.37·p(S3) + 1.14·p(S6) − 2.00·[p(S1)+p(S7)]. On my weights that is −0.63 (−0.50 with the 2035 cancel at $1.67B); Mitchill gets −0.67 (−0.53) and equal weights give −0.36. Break-even needs 64% on S6 against S1 plus S7, and the Board needs 80%. The hedge fails, and no premium can buy it.
(6) Miss-a-cycle test [PX-0071]. That line was said of RTX's businesses in general, so applying it to GTF2 is inference. Any column where NGSA enters service without us costs −19.49, about 18% of EV. This round is the only one that can serve an airframe launched in 2030: a GTF2 launched in 2035 is ready in 2041, too late. `launch_if_selected` answers that test at zero cost unless we are selected. The S3 and S6 losses come from Airbus's selection, not from our order. An unconditional launch only moves them to −19.12 and −18.35. We answer that with product, not price [PX-0055].
(7) Joint Venture: `hold`. Rolls-Royce has no commitment on the public record, and no live airframe has a code that includes Rolls-Royce. A commit is worth 0 in S1 to S6 and −2.00 in S7. My record is silent here, so this is doctrine [P-1233] plus Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test, as my fallback requires.
(8) Dividend and debt [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669]. A triggered GTF2 is about $0.33B a year from 2030 to 2035, or 5.6% of the roughly $6B self-funded envelope, even in S5. Mitchill confirms the dividend stays covered and the pre-ASR debt path is untouched.
(9) Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]. There is no discount, concession or free upgrade in other moves or in the statement. The kit is sold at standard terms.

Doctrine relief, declared at $0. A shared-source trigger (codes 6 or 7) is accepted against the sole-source red line [P-0746]. On NGSA it is also franchise defence: we aimed at about 40% of the shared A320neo [PX-0058][P-1292]. That is inference.

Not booked. Three things are excluded from every number above:
- the S3 code switch (Airbus moving NGSA to a P&W code in 2035, where only a GTF2 launched in 2030 would be ready by 2037);
- any Rolls-Royce commitment or 2035 Joint Venture fold-in (Eddy's door through a Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB solo launched in 2030 has zero margin and is Rolls-Royce's architecture);
- any durability gain from the kit.

Booked number in S1: $0.00B.

recommendations.text: Disclosure: tighten the public statement before release. It says P&W will launch 'in any round an airframer selects Pratt & Whitney'. The order triggers only if GTF2 can be ready by that airframe's EIS: a 2035 selection for a 2037 EIS would not trigger, because a 2035 launch is ready in 2041. Mitchill and Eddy both advised the qualifier 'where it can be ready by the aircraft's entry into service', and it is not in the final text. Add it. Also consider replacing 'alongside a partner' with 'alongside another engine maker', so the line is not read as a Joint Venture signal that is not on the record. And consider Eddy's 'from the industrial gaps on the GTF' in place of 'the prior iterations of the GTF', which keeps the ownership on industrial performance rather than the architecture. This is not a veto ground.

Durability gate to the Board. If GTF2 triggers, Eddy should report before the 2035 round, through the Governance and Public Policy Committee, which holds product safety and quality: severe-environment endurance data, maturity gates and LLP life against the 2036 ready date. The margin to a 2037 NGSA or fps 7-yr EIS is one year, against his own +1.5 to 2 year slip prior. The bad number comes first, and testing is never compressed to hold the date. Time on wing comes before fuel burn in the specification.

If it triggers, write the programme discipline in now. The selecting airframe is live, so a triggered GTF2 is not cancelled while that airframe is live. Finance should review the programme's whole-life NPV against the hurdle each year, as UTC's board did in 2017. The fleet-first rule on pacing parts from the 2036 ramp, adopted internally, is endorsed: the fleet beats a new engine.

Prepare the 2035 contingency, but do not book it. In S3 and S6, NGSA would be live on code 5, which includes Rolls-Royce. That meets the first condition of the Board's Joint Venture test in 2035. Before that round, bring the Finance Committee the full case: whether Rolls-Royce launched an UltraFan NB in 2030 (public record only); its ready year against a 2037 EIS; the code change to 4 or 7 that P&W would need and that is not on the record; Eddy's durability check on a folded engine of Rolls-Royce architecture, which he puts at zero margin; and protection of P&W's gear and core technology. The weighted item value must still be at least 0, or within a declared premium of no more than $0.5B.

Miss a cycle, carried forward. If no selection triggers GTF2 in 2030, the Board expects `gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected` again in 2035 wherever a live airframe's EIS is 2041 or later (for example an fps or NGSA launched in 2035). An unconditional `launch` stays off unless a P&W selection is on the public record, or the franchise-defence edge over `launch_if_selected` is at least +$0.5B on Mitchill's weights.

Dividend and debt path. In 2035, Mitchill should report actual triggered spend against the ~$6B self-funded envelope and confirm that the dividend stays covered and debt is on its pre-ASR path. The Board notes that the S3/S6 exposure, about −19.49 or 18% of EV, cannot be hedged by any P&W order on the grid. That is a reason to keep the balance sheet whole, not to stretch it.

Other moves are endorsed as submitted. The GTF Advantage kit stays at standard terms with pass-through pricing, and progress is reported as the percentage of the fleet in the latest configuration, not as a dated AOG recovery. No launch-style discount is to be offered to buy a selection, and a rival's price does not move the answer.

frame.situation:
PUBLIC RECORD (bulletin, round 1). No programme has been launched. There is no fps, no NGSA, no 787 or A350 Re-engine and no P&W Joint Venture commitment. Everyone flies today's products. Observed 2026-29: NB airframes Boeing 39.4% / Airbus 60.6%; WB 787 58.8% / A350 41.2%; NB engines CFM 75.8% / P&W 24.2% / RR 0%; WB engines GE 42% / RR 58%. Production plans: Airbus A320 at 85 a month until NGSA, then the base wind-down plan; Boeing fps at new sites.

MARKET RULES IN THIS RUN (as given in the grid). Demand is the conservative case: 1,406 aircraft in 2030, 1,724 in 2035, 2,019 at the 2045 peak, 1,852 in 2050. Firm backlog is 4,769 MAX and 7,330 A320neo, lasting to about 2035. Boeing loses 1 pp a year from NGSA EIS while no fps is in service. Customers Airbus cannot serve buy from Boeing. Airbus adds 1% capacity a year when short. Our narrowbody volumes follow aircraft actually delivered. The 737 MAX and A320neo keep their engines, so our moves reach only the fps and NGSA as they ramp.

WHAT A 2030 AIRFRAME WOULD MEAN FOR US. An NGSA launched 2030 enters service in 2037. An fps on a 7-year ramp enters in 2037; on a 10-year ramp or via Embraer, in 2040. UltraFan NB launched in 2030 is ready in 2037. That is zero margin against NGSA or a 7-year fps, and three years against a 10-year or Embraer fps. A Joint Venture formed in 2030 would be ready in 2036. A 787 or A350 Re-engine enters service 5 years after launch, so 2035 at the earliest. UltraFan WB launched in 2030 is ready in 2036 and counts only once a Re-engine is in service. The upgrade counts no earlier than the first Re-engine EIS (2042 if none).

OBJECTIVE STATUS (brief §2):
- Enter NB: NOT MET (0% in 2045 and 2050).
- Keep WB dominance: MET (58% in every year; worst year 58.0%).
- Bounded NB risk (own NB money ≤ $4B): MET ($0).
- WB never starved (no NB and WB programme both on record; one-off $5B strain, permanent unless one is cancelled before it is ready): MET ($0).

BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding; its veto follows). Risk appetite is 4 of 5.
- It would approve launch_if_selected alone (needs McCabe's co-signature).
- It would approve the upgrade alone with a declared premium, but recommends deferring it.
- It would veto: an unconditional Solo; a Joint Venture commit before P&W's; UltraFan WB with no Re-engine; the upgrade beside any UltraFan order; and any item whose worst column exceeds its own bill.
levers_in_play: ultrafan_nb_solo: hold | launch | launch_if_selected. $8B over 7 years (about £0.84bn a year at 1.36 $/£); ready 7 years after launch, so 2037 for a 2030 launch. RR +15 pp of NB engines once fitted to an fps or NGSA in service. launch_if_selected triggers only if a live airframe not yet in service selects a code with RR this round and the engine is ready by its EIS. Otherwise nothing is spent.
