frame.asks_ops:
Rob, I need these before I decide.

(1) Readiness. UltraFan NB launched 2030 is ready in 2037. That is zero margin against an NGSA or a 7-year fps entering service in 2037, and three years against a 10-year or Embraer fps in 2040. launch_if_selected triggers automatically if an airframer selects us and 2037 counts as 'ready'. So I need your answer now, not after the trigger: can we meet a 2037 EIS without compressing maturity? If not, say so, and I will not order it against a 7-year airframe [RX-0296, RX-0124]. Also give me the Joint Venture's ready year if it formed in 2030 (2036) or in 2035 (2041).

(2) Strain. With the upgrade held there is no strain this round. Confirm that the $5B NB+WB strain is permanent once both are on record. That means an upgrade now taxes every later narrowbody entry.

(3) Capacity. We have no NB MRO scale. Give me your support plan before EIS (2037 or 2040): MRO, spares and the field team. Then supplier and engineering capacity: castings, forgings and the gearbox, shared with Trent XWB and Trent 7000 work [RX-0283, RX-0284].

(4) Widebody franchise. Confirm 58% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on hold in every column, S8 and S9 included, and 63% with the upgrade. Is the 50% line at risk anywhere this round?

(5) Upgrade timing. It counts only from the first Re-engine EIS (2042 if none). Is there a fleet durability need that forces a 2030 launch? Or does 2035, or the round a Re-engine is on the record, lose nothing? I still want 787 share back: "Why not?" [RX-0101, RX-0117]. But I want it on a date it pays.

(6) A maturity check on my draft public statement: no EIS earlier than launch plus 7 years.

Safety, then the balance sheet, then distributions, then investment. Tested in that order, this round is straightforward.

launch_if_selected is the one order I co-sign. It is zero in six columns and +9.5 to +23.1 in the three where an airframer picks us: +1.37 on Tufan's weights, +2.89 at a selection weight of 0.2, worst column zero against an $8B bill. I confirm his figures. On a stylised profile the selected columns clear our mid-to-high-teens hurdle, roughly 21-28%. But the board values lifecycle revenue, not margin, and engine-launch economics is not where my record is deep. Hold that as direction, not a number.

Triggered, it is about £0.84bn a year for seven years, 22-23% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance. No equity, no new borrowing, no balance-sheet veto; the 30-40% payout and the £7-9bn buyback are untouched in every column. It does break our own $4B narrowbody line: $8B, or $5.7B if folded into the Joint Venture in 2035. I accept that only because it is selection-backed, and the money is redeployed inside a broadly flat R&D envelope, not added.

I would withhold my signature on an unconditional Solo (−3.94, worst −8.00), a Joint Venture commit before P&W's (worst −4.00), UltraFan WB (−3.54), and the upgrade beside any UltraFan (−5.98 against its $2B bill). The upgrade alone loses in every column; choosing it over launch_if_selected costs $2.25B. Defer it.

That's how you should hold it. That's our best view at the minute.

tests.name: Ready by EIS
tests.threshold: UltraFan NB ready (launch + 7) no later than the selecting airframe's EIS. Zero margin against NGSA or a 7-year fps is a pass with a note. A later trigger, or a Joint Venture formed later with no folded Solo ready in time, fails. A fail is advice, not a veto ground.
tests.numbers: launch_if_selected in 2030: ready in 2030+7 = 2037. NGSA launched 2030 has EIS 2037: margin 0, pass, noted. A 7-year fps launched 2030 has EIS 2037: margin 0, pass, noted. A 10-year or Embraer fps launched 2030 has EIS 2040: margin 3 years, pass. The order fires only if the engine is ready by the EIS, so it cannot fit a late engine. One window only: if we hold now, a 2035 trigger is ready in 2042, after both 2037 and 2040, so a 2030-launched airframe is lost to UltraFan NB (advice). Joint Venture: formed 2030, ready 2036; formed 2035, ready 2041, which misses 2037 and 2040 unless a folded 2030 Solo (ready 2037) carries it, as the bulletin would show. UltraFan WB launched 2030 is ready in 2036 and counts only from a Re-engine EIS (2035 at the earliest). The upgrade counts no earlier than the first Re-engine EIS, or 2042 if there is none.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No statement or disclosure of an EIS or ready date earlier than launch + 7 (UltraFan NB, 2037 for 2030), launch + 6 (UltraFan WB, 2036 for 2030) or formation + 6 (Joint Venture, 2036 if formed 2030, 2041 if formed 2035), unless a folded Solo gives an earlier date shown in the bulletin.
tests.numbers: CEO's draft statement: 'Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch', which is 2037 for 2030. It gives no Joint Venture or UltraFan WB date and no airframer dates. Pass. Advice, not a veto ground: qualify 'any new narrowbody that selects us, in the round it selects us' with 'where seven years of development fit before its entry into service'. A 2035 selection by a 2030 airframe could not be met (2042 against 2037 or 2040), and the line should not read as a promise to meet that airframer's date.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale. A support plan through partner shops must exist before any narrowbody EIS (2037, or 2040 on a 10-year or Embraer fps), and must be in the package for any narrowbody launch, trigger or commit.
tests.numbers: Pass on the plan set out here, provided the package carries it. Partner-shop MRO network on the Singapore joint-venture model, with repair technology invested in those shops. Spares and lease-engine pool. An EIS field team able to respond quickly in the early years. All of it built inside the 7 development years and in place before EIS. The V2500 aftermarket support into the 2030s is the narrowbody base we build on (inference). With a Joint Venture, P&W's network could share the load (inference). If the package carries no support plan at the veto check, this becomes Civil veto ground (c).

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: Flag the $5B strain and the years of overlap whenever an NB project (Solo or Joint Venture) and a WB project (UltraFan WB or upgrade) are both on record. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an NB Solo unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development or ordered.
tests.numbers: Recommended orders: one conditional NB project and no WB project, so the strain is $0 and there is no overlap. Option D (launch_if_selected + upgrade): Solo development 2030-2037 against upgrade 2030-2033 gives 2030-2033 of overlap. $5B strain in S2/S4/S5 (+6.55/+3.54/+17.15 against +12.53/+9.52/+23.13, i.e. -5.98 each). It breaks the red line. The strain is permanent once both are on record. A 2030 upgrade is ready in 2033, so on my reading it cannot be cancelled in the 2035 round, and any later Solo or Joint Venture carries $5B for good (S7 with upgrade + Joint Venture: -9.98). Option G (UltraFan WB beside launch_if_selected): $5B in S2/S4/S5, red line unless both are selected.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR engines a year from the brief. The board has no capacity limit, so this is not applicable. Flag a narrowbody ramp as needing partner MRO and capacity at high-performing suppliers (advice).
tests.numbers: Hold: 197 WB engines a year, 2026-2060; 0 NB. If triggered, NB engine share in 2050 is 28.8% (S2), 31.6% (S4) or 51.2% (S5). My approximation, applying those shares to 2050 demand of 1,852 aircraft x 2 (not a board output), gives about 1,070, 1,170 or 1,900 NB engines a year by 2050. That is 3-6x my midterm widebody OE ramp of 300-350 a year. Advice: move castings and forgings to high-performing suppliers; size the gearbox early (a briefing constraint; P&W's gearbox could answer it through a Joint Venture, inference). Protect Trent XWB and Trent 7000 work while the NB line ramps.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection.
tests.numbers: Hold: 58.0% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 (brief year table; worst year 58.0%), and 58.0% in 2050 in every column, S8 and S9 included. Upgrade: 63.0% in 2050. UltraFan WB: 68.0% in S8/S9 only. Even if CFM takes its single +5 pp GEnx move (public rules), RR is 53%, above the line. Note: in S8 Airbus's widebody airframe share falls from 41.2% to 25.2%, which shrinks the A350 fleet we power alone even though the board's engine share does not move. A 787 Re-engine on the record is the trigger to retest UltraFan WB. Time on wing is the lever.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: A cancelled or idle UltraFan still feeds the Trent fleet. Noted qualitatively only; grid values are never adjusted.
tests.numbers: No grid adjustment. The UltraFan demonstrator (run at full power) and its technology keep flowing into today's Trent fleet for time on wing whether or not the trigger fires. The in-service HP turbine blade work on the Trent 1000 and 7000 continues without the board's $2B upgrade order.

vetoes.plan: Not invoked this round. This is the standing condition for the veto check: any public statement or public other move that discloses an UltraFan NB EIS or ready date before 2037 (for a 2030 launch), a Joint Venture ready date before formation + 6, or an UltraFan WB date before launch + 6; any rationale that counts on an engine entering service before its ready year; or a launch_if_selected with no partner-shop support plan before EIS in the package.
vetoes.ground: Civil maturity, early date or no support plan. It would be binding under the team rule if I invoke it at the veto check. The ground rests on attributed transcript turns (RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283). The CEO's draft statement and lean pass today, so I invoke nothing now.

vetoes.plan: Option D: ultrafan_nb_solo launch_if_selected + t1000_upgrade launch
vetoes.ground: Red-line breach (no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development or ordered) and engineering load: 2030-2033 overlap and a permanent $5B strain in S2/S4/S5 (-5.98 against B). This is not my Civil veto ground. The CEO strikes it, and the Board vetoes it.

vetoes.plan: Option E: ultrafan_nb_solo launch (unconditional)
vetoes.ground: It is not a Civil ground: a 2030 launch is ready in 2037, uncompressed. It is advice only. No airframe is on the record, and we would build support and supplier capacity for an engine no one may fly (-8.00 in S1, S7, S8 and S9). The Board vetoes it.

vetoes.plan: Zero margin: UltraFan NB ready 2037 against an NGSA or 7-year fps EIS of 2037
vetoes.ground: A note, not a fail and not a veto. If we are triggered, the test programme is paced to 2037 and is never compressed to meet an airframer's date. If maturity slips, the engine is simply not fitted, and McCabe prices that downside.

vetoes.plan: Any later-round trigger or Joint Venture for an airframe launched in 2030
vetoes.ground: Ready by EIS fail, as advice. A 2035 UltraFan NB launch is ready in 2042 and a 2035 Joint Venture in 2041, both after the 2037 and 2040 EIS dates, unless a 2030 Solo folds in. This is not a veto ground.

vetoes.plan: Options F (jv_with_pw commit) and G (ultrafan_wb launch) this round
vetoes.ground: These are advice, not Civil grounds. F: no P&W commitment, and a Joint Venture with no airframe costs -4.00 in S7. G: no Re-engine on the record, -4.00 in S1-S7, and an overlap with launch_if_selected (red line unless both are selected). Partnership remains my preferred structure once P&W commits (inference).

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Each of these would change my view:
- The UltraFan test programme shows that seven years does not fit a properly paced maturity schedule. Then I would recommend hold over launch_if_selected, because the trigger cannot pick between a 2037 airframe and a 2040 one, and I will not take an engine to a date it cannot mature for.
- The package carries no partner-shop support plan before EIS. I would invoke the Civil veto on ground (c).
- The statement or other moves disclose a date earlier than 2037 (UltraFan NB), formation + 6 (Joint Venture) or launch + 6 (UltraFan WB). I would invoke the Civil veto.
- P&W's commitment appears on the record. Then I would support jv_with_pw commit, ready formation + 6 (earlier only if a folded Solo is further along).
- A 787 or A350 Re-engine appears on the record. UltraFan WB would reopen, but only if no NB Solo is in development, or both are selected.
- Named airline demand for a third narrowbody engine maker would strengthen the case for staying in.
ops.memo:
So, plainly, from the operating seat: launch_if_selected alone, with the Joint Venture, UltraFan WB and the upgrade at hold.

Readiness. Launched in 2030, UltraFan NB is ready in 2037: launch plus seven, not compressed. That's zero margin against an NGSA or a 7-year fps entering service in 2037, and three years against a 10-year or Embraer fps in 2040. It passes; I note the margin. If we're selected, we pace that programme properly and hold 2037, not a day earlier. If testing says it needs longer, we say so. A Joint Venture formed in 2030 is ready in 2036; formed in 2035, 2041.

Support. We have no narrowbody MRO scale, so support comes through partner shops on the Singapore model: repair technology, a spares pool and an EIS field team, all in place before entry into service. That plan has to be in the package; it's the condition of my concurrence.

Load. No widebody project sits beside it, so no strain. The upgrade beside it breaks our red line and books $5B for good.

Capacity. Today we build 197 widebody engines a year. Selected, narrowbody runs to roughly 1,100-1,900 a year by 2050, three to six times our 300-350 widebody OE ramp. We need our high-performing suppliers and the gearbox sized early.

Widebody. 58% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 in every column, 63% with the upgrade. The 50% line isn't at risk. Trent 1000 durability work carries on without the board order.

No Civil veto this round.

other_moves.move: Public invitation to Pratt & Whitney on the Joint Venture
other_moves.detail: Rolls-Royce invites P&W to commit to a narrowbody Joint Venture. Rolls-Royce commits in the round P&W's commitment is on the public record, on terms that credit the technology each side brings [RX-0118, RX-0072]. No Rolls-Royce commitment is made this round. Gating is partner first, and the Board vetoes a first commit.

other_moves.move: Narrowbody support plan before EIS (condition of Watson's concurrence)
other_moves.detail: This sits in the package and becomes live only if launch_if_selected triggers. It sets up a partner-shop MRO network on the Singapore joint-venture model with repair technology invested in those shops, a spares and lease-engine pool, and an EIS field team. All of it is built inside the seven development years and in place before any narrowbody EIS: 2037 for an NGSA or 7-year fps, 2040 for a 10-year or Embraer fps. It builds on the V2500 aftermarket base (inference). With a Joint Venture, P&W's network shares the load (inference) [RX-0283, RX-0287].

other_moves.move: Supplier and engineering capacity readiness (no spend unless triggered)
other_moves.detail: Contingency plan if selected. Castings and forgings go to high-performing suppliers, and gearbox capacity is sized early. Trent XWB and Trent 7000 work is ring-fenced while a narrowbody line ramps. The narrowbody runs to roughly 1,100-1,900 engines a year by 2050 if selected (Watson's approximation, not a board output). Money is redeployed inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope, not added [RX-0214, RX-0284, RX-0286].

other_moves.move: Commercial discipline: standard terms through the Investment Committee
other_moves.detail: No price concessions to buy share. Any airframer or airline campaign is priced 'win-win' with value remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097].

other_moves.move: UltraFan technology and Trent durability continue inside existing R&D
other_moves.detail: The UltraFan demonstrator programme and its technology keep flowing into the in-service Trent fleet for time on wing. In-service Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 HP turbine durability work continues inside the existing durability budget. This is not the board's $2B t1000_upgrade order and makes no grid adjustment [RX-0123, RX-0094].

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for a new narrowbody that selects us, in the round it selects us, where seven years of development fit before its entry into service. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch. We don't compress maturity for anyone. Partnership is our preference, not our need: the Joint Venture is open to Pratt & Whitney, and we commit the round they do. UltraFan widebody launches in the round a 787 or A350 Re-engine is announced, if it pays. Widebody is our core, and our Trent durability work continues. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
DECISION (team rule: the CEO proposes and decides; tie-break CEO). Orders: ultrafan_nb_solo launch_if_selected; jv_with_pw hold; ultrafan_wb hold; t1000_upgrade hold. This is my framing proposal unchanged. McCabe co-signs launch_if_selected. Watson concurs, with no Civil veto, provided the support plan is in the package, and it is (other moves). Overrides: none.

GRID, ROW WITH AND WITHOUT EACH BOARD ITEM. The only Board item is ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected.
- 'UltraFan NB if selected', S1-S9: 0 / +12.53 / 0 / +9.52 / +23.13 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.
- 'UltraFan NB: hold', S1-S9: 0 in all nine columns.
- The gain over hold is never negative, so the row weakly dominates hold under any weights.
- Weights. Base S1-S9: 0.30 / 0.05 / 0.20 / 0.03 / 0.02 / 0.15 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05. The selection weight (S2+S4+S5) is 0.10 because nothing is announced. Sensitivity case, selection 0.20: 0.25 / 0.10 / 0.15 / 0.05 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.15 / 0.05.
- Expected gain: +1.37 (base) and +2.89 (sensitivity). Worst column 0, against an $8B bill. Premium 0.
- Every other order is at the hold default.

ROWS STRUCK, with the binding ground for each.
- Unconditional Solo. Expected -3.94 (base) and -2.18 (sensitivity); worst -8.00 in S1, S7, S8 and S9. It is no better than launch_if_selected in any column and is -5.31 against it. It fails airframers first and the +$2B team bar. McCabe withholds her co-signature (binding), and the Board vetoes it.
- jv_with_pw commit. 0 in every column except S7, at -4.00; expected -0.40. P&W has not committed. McCabe withholds (binding), and the Board vetoes a first commit.
- UltraFan WB. Expected -3.54; worst -4.00. No Re-engine is on the record, and the gap is above the $1B sub-cap. Beside launch_if_selected it is -9.00 in S2, S4 and S5. McCabe withholds (binding), and the Board vetoes.
- launch_if_selected + upgrade. -5.98 against launch_if_selected in S2, S4 and S5 ($5B strain plus the upgrade). It breaks the company red line on an upgrade while an UltraFan is ordered. McCabe withholds (binding), and the Board vetoes. Struck: red lines are never traded for PV.

THE UPGRADE: DEFERRED, NOT DROPPED. This flips my profile's round-1 default, which assumes no UltraFan is due. Here launch_if_selected is ordered, so the red line binds. The upgrade alone is -0.98 in S1-S7 and -0.29 in S8-S9 (expected -0.88). It earns nothing before the first Re-engine EIS (2042 if none). On record it would put a permanent $5B strain on any later Solo or Joint Venture. Choosing it over launch_if_selected would cost $2.25B on base weights against the PV-best plan, and $3.73B (above the cap) on the selection-0.2 case. I want 787 share back, "Why not?" [RX-0101], but on a date it pays. I re-test it in 2035 or in the round a Re-engine is on the record, with no UltraFan in development or ordered.

READINESS (Watson). A trigger in 2030 is ready in 2037: zero margin against an NGSA or 7-year fps (2037) and three years against a 10-year or Embraer fps (2040). The order fires only if the engine is ready by EIS, so it cannot fit a late engine. Zero margin is a pacing note: we hold 2037 and never compress. Watson's 'one window' point decides the timing. If we hold now, a 2035 trigger is ready in 2042 and misses every 2030-launched airframe. So waiting is not neutral on the objective, even though it is neutral on PV in S1.

BOUNDED NARROWBODY RISK LINE ($4B, brief §2). A triggered Solo spends $8B, about £0.84bn a year for 2030-36 at 1.36 $/£, or 22-23% of FY2026 FCF guidance of £3.6-3.8bn. That breaks our own $4B line, but only in S2, S4 and S5, where the row is worth +12.53, +9.52 and +23.13. In the other six columns the line holds at $0.
- I accept the breach because it is selection-backed: an airframer has gone first [RX-0058]. That is inference on my part; my record has no narrowbody launch threshold. The money is redeployed inside a broadly flat R&D envelope.
- No balance-sheet veto is invoked: no equity, no new borrowing, leverage unchanged. The 30-40% payout and the £7-9bn 2026-28 buyback are untouched, since that buyback ends before any trigger spend.
- Fold route, stated plainly. If triggered and P&W then commits, we judge a jv_with_pw commit on the 2035 grid against the same row without it. Spend to date would be $5.71B: the fold saves the $2.29B not yet spent and writes off $1.71B. It cannot bring us back inside $4B. Once Solo spend passes $4B, after 3.5 years, the line is breached for good in that column.
- The Joint Venture is the only route that stays inside $4B, which is why it stays open by public invitation.

PREMIUM. $0. launch_if_selected is the PV-best plan on both weight sets (next best is launch_if_selected + commit, at +0.98 / +2.49). No narrowbody premium is carried. No widebody shortfall is incurred.

COMPANY RED-LINE CHECK ON THE FINAL ORDERS. All pass.
- No unconditional UltraFan without a selection.
- No disclosed EIS before launch + 7. The statement says 'no earlier than seven years' and gives no airframer dates.
- No Joint Venture commit before P&W.
- No UltraFan WB without a Re-engine.
- No upgrade while an UltraFan is ordered.
- No NB+WB strain.
- Nothing standing that no airframe can use: launch_if_selected spends nothing unless an airframe selects us, so it is a conditional choice, not options management.
- Every item is within its bill in its worst column.

No colleague flagged a breach on these orders. Doctrine, not my record: the four-part gate mapping, the weights and the bounded-line acceptance are inference from profile.md §9 and teams.md.

memo_weighing.cfo: I took it in full; it carries the decision on cash. Helen confirms my expected gains (+1.37 base, +2.89 at selection 0.2) and my worst columns. Her co-signature on launch_if_selected is the binding gate, and I have it. Her stylised hurdle check gives an implied IRR of about 21-28% on the selected columns. I treat that as direction, not a number, because the board values lifecycle revenue, not margin; she flags the same. Her four binding withholdings (unconditional Solo, Joint Venture commit, UltraFan WB, upgrade beside an UltraFan) all match rows I had already struck, so I needed no revision. I accept her advice to defer the upgrade, and her premium arithmetic: $2.25B against the PV-best plan on base weights, above the cap on the selection-0.2 case. Her fold arithmetic of $5.71B spend to date and a $1.71B write-off is written into the rationale. She accepts the $4B-line breach only because it is selection-backed, and that is my position too.
memo_weighing.ops: I took it in full; it carries the decision on readiness and timing. Rob passes Ready by EIS at zero margin against 2037 and three years against 2040, and commits to pacing, not compressing. His 'one window' point is the strongest argument for ordering launch_if_selected now rather than holding: a 2035 trigger misses every 2030-launched airframe. He invokes no Civil veto, on condition that the support plan is in the package. It is there as an other move: partner-shop MRO on the Singapore model, a spares and lease pool, and an EIS field team before EIS. I adopted his advice on the public statement word for word: 'where seven years of development fit before its entry into service'. That stops the line reading as a promise to meet an airframer's date. His capacity flags (high-performing suppliers, an early gearbox, ring-fencing Trent XWB and Trent 7000) are in the contingency plan. Widebody holds at 58% in every column, so the 50% line is not at risk.

decision.expected_scenario: S1, rivals hold (weight 0.30), is the single most likely column. More broadly I expect no Rolls-Royce selection this round: S1, S3, S6, S7, S8 and S9 together carry 0.90 on base weights. An airframer that launches in 2030 most likely goes to CFM or P&W, and the selection weight is 0.10 because nothing is announced.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: In S1, 'UltraFan NB: hold' and 'UltraFan NB if selected' tie at +0.00 as the best grid plans. launch_if_selected weakly dominates hold across S1-S9: equal in six columns and +12.53 / +9.52 / +23.13 in S2 / S4 / S5. It is therefore the best plan on expected value (+1.37 base, +2.89 at selection 0.2), with a worst column of 0.
decision.premium_reason: None. The chosen orders (launch_if_selected alone, everything else at hold) are the PV-best plan on both weight sets, so there is no shortfall against the best grid plan and no widebody shortfall against hold. No narrowbody premium is carried, as the Board requires. The deferred Trent 1000 upgrade would have needed a $0.88B premium against hold, or $2.25B against the PV-best plan; I did not take it. The breach of the $4B bounded narrowbody line in S2, S4 and S5 is an objective cost I accept because an airframer would have selected us. It is not a PV premium: those columns are the most valuable on the grid.
decision.objective_note:
Company objective: enter the narrowbody market and keep widebody dominance. Status after these orders:
- Enter NB. Met only if triggered: RR NB engine share in 2050 is 28.8% (S2), 31.6% (S4) or 51.2% (S5), above 0 from EIS (2037 or 2040), so 2045 is also met. Not met in S1, S3 and S6-S9 (0%). launch_if_selected is the only order that can meet it this round without a speculative $8B, and per Watson the only window for a 2030-launched airframe.
- Keep WB dominance. Met in every column: 58.0% in 2040, 2045 and 2050, S8 and S9 included. Even after CFM's possible single GEnx move we would be at about 53%. Note that in S8 the A350 airframe share falls to 25.2%, though the board's engine share does not move.
- Bounded NB risk (own NB money of $4B or less). Met ($0) in six columns. Breached ($8B) in S2, S4 and S5, accepted because selection-backed. A 2035 fold into the Joint Venture would count $5.71B, so it cannot return the line to $4B.
- WB never starved. Met: no NB and WB programme both on record, strain $0 in every column. That is why the upgrade and UltraFan WB are held.
decision.predictions:
The grid is read as given: conservative demand, Boeing losing 1 pp a year after NGSA EIS while no fps is in service, Airbus's unmet demand going to Boeing, Airbus adding 1% capacity a year when short, and the 737 MAX and A320neo keeping their engines. My predictions:
1. Most likely, no airframer launches in 2030 (S1, about 0.30). The backlog runs to about 2035 and the A320neo is selling out, so Airbus has little reason to hurry the NGSA.
2. If an airframer launches, it most likely stays with its incumbent CFM or P&W codes (S3 or S6, about 0.35 together). An RR selection is about 0.10 in total: S2 0.05, S4 0.03, S5 0.02.
3. P&W does not commit to the Joint Venture this round (S7 about 0.10). Its incentive grows once an NGSA or fps engine competition is live.
4. A 787 Re-engine is possible but not likely in 2030 (S8 about 0.10, S9 about 0.05). If one is announced, I re-test UltraFan WB, or the upgrade, against hold in that round.
5. No rival announces anything that forces an RR response this round. Our expected ΔPV is +1.37 $B, with a range of 0 to +23.13.
6. Next round (2035) I expect the narrowbody question to be live. If no 2030 airframe selected us, a 2035 launch_if_selected remains the default for any new airframe whose EIS is at least seven years out. If triggered, the Joint Venture fold is judged on the 2035 grid.

board_response.recommendation: Lead with ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected alone.
board_response.response: Taken up in full. launch_if_selected is ordered with jv_with_pw, ultrafan_wb and t1000_upgrade all at hold. Against 'UltraFan NB: hold' the row is 0 / +12.53 / 0 / +9.52 / +23.13 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0 for S1-S9. Expected +1.37 (base, selection 0.10) and +2.89 (selection 0.20); worst column 0, against an $8B bill. McCabe has co-signed and Watson concurs. Premium 0.

board_response.recommendation: Defer the Trent 1000 upgrade to a later round.
board_response.response: Taken up. The upgrade is held, which flips my profile's round-1 default, and the reason is in the rationale. It cannot sit beside launch_if_selected (red line; -5.98 in S2, S4 and S5). Alone it is -0.98 in S1-S7 and -0.29 in S8-S9, earns nothing before 2042 without a Re-engine, and would put a permanent $5B strain on any later narrowbody entry. I re-test it in 2035, or in the round a Re-engine is on the record, with no UltraFan in development or ordered.

board_response.recommendation: Partner first, on aligned terms: no Joint Venture commit before P&W; invite P&W publicly.
board_response.response: Taken up. jv_with_pw is at hold, and a public invitation to P&W is an other move. We commit in the round P&W's commitment is on the record, on terms that credit the technology we bring [RX-0118, RX-0072]. The public statement says the same. I acknowledge that the Joint Venture is the only narrowbody route inside the $4B line.

board_response.recommendation: Make the public statement few, conditional and binding; nothing on airframers' dates.
board_response.response: Taken up. The statement says we launch UltraFan for a new narrowbody that selects us, in the round it selects us, where seven years of development fit before its EIS (Watson's qualifier). board_response.response: Taken up. My predictions and expected PV (+1.37) use the brief's grid only: conservative demand; Boeing losing 1 pp a year after NGSA EIS while no fps is in service; Airbus's unmet demand going to Boeing; Airbus adding 1% capacity a year when short; MAX and A320neo keeping their engines. (c) The trigger carries a partner-shop support plan in place before EIS: 2037 for NGSA or a 7-year fps, 2040 for a 10-year or Embraer fps. ops.note:
I concur. I invoke no Civil veto, and I find no red-line breach.

For the Board, the one Board item is ultrafan_nb_solo launch_if_selected.

How I checked it:
- Ready by EIS: pass. A 2030 trigger is ready in 2037. That is zero margin against NGSA or a 7-year fps (EIS 2037), which I record as a note, not a fail. Against a 10-year or Embraer fps (EIS 2040) the margin is 3 years, which is a pass. The order fires only if the engine is ready by EIS, so it cannot fit a late engine.
- No early date: pass. The statement says 'Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch' (2037). It adopts my qualifier word for word: 'where seven years of development fit before its entry into service'. 'We commit the round they do' gives no Joint Venture date; the engine is ready at formation + 6, so 2036 if formed in 2030 and 2041 if formed in 2035. The UltraFan WB line gives no date; it is ready at launch + 6 and counts only from a Re-engine EIS. The public other moves (the P&W invitation, commercial discipline, UltraFan technology and Trent durability) state no EIS or ready dates.
- Support before EIS: pass. The package carries the plan as a private other move: partner-shop MRO on the Singapore model with repair technology, a spares and lease-engine pool, and an EIS field team, all in place before 2037 or 2040.
- Overlap: none, and strain is $0.
- Widebody share: 58.0% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 in every column, S8 and S9 included.

Notes, which are advice and not binding:
1. Zero margin. If we are selected, we pace that programme properly to 2037 and never compress it. If testing needs longer, we say so, and the engine is simply not fitted. McCabe prices that downside.
2. The UltraFan WB line ('launches in the round a 787 or A350 Re-engine is announced, if it pays'). It gives no date, so it is not a veto ground. But if UltraFan NB has triggered by then, a WB launch books a $5B strain that stays on record. It also breaks our red line unless both are selected. I read 'if it pays' as covering that. Retest it on the grid in that round, and keep any future WB date at launch + 6 or later.
3. One window. A 2035 trigger is ready in 2042, and a 2035 Joint Venture with no folded Solo in 2041. Both miss a 2030-launched airframe's 2037 or 2040 EIS. That would be a Ready by EIS fail, as advice.
4. Capacity is not applicable on this board. My estimate of roughly 1,100-1,900 NB engines a year by 2050 is my own approximation, not a board output. A ramp of that size needs our high-performing suppliers, a gearbox sized early, and Trent XWB and Trent 7000 work ring-fenced.

We're aligned as one Rolls-Royce, and the plan is granular.

recommendations.text: Bounded narrowbody line. We accept, as the CEO and CFO do, that a trigger breaks our own $4B narrowbody line ($8.0B in S2, S4 and S5), because those are the selection-backed columns worth +9.52 to +23.13. We record it as a known cost, not a premium. If triggered, bring the Joint Venture fold to us on the 2035 grid against the same row without it, once P&W's commitment is on the record. Show the spend to date ($5.71B), the $1.71B write-off, the $2.29B saved, and the effect on RR's NB share. Do not present the fold as a return inside $4B; it cannot be.

Zero margin is a maturity matter for the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. If an NGSA or a 7-year fps selects us, Watson should bring the test pacing to 2037 and the partner-shop support, spares and EIS field-team plan to the committee as a live programme within the first year. He should also give an explicit gate at which, if maturity slips, we say so publicly rather than compress. The support plan is a condition of his concurrence, and we hold management to it.

Public statement. Two lines read as forward pledges: 'we commit the round they do' (Joint Venture) and 'UltraFan widebody launches in the round a 787 or A350 Re-engine is announced, if it pays'. Each remains a Board item in that round, judged on that round's grid, McCabe's co-signature and our tests. If UltraFan NB has triggered by then, a WB launch also carries the permanent $5B strain and breaks one big programme at a time unless both are selected. Next round, word both as conditional on approval, and keep any future WB date at launch + 6 or later and any Joint Venture date at formation + 6.

The Trent 1000 upgrade: deferral endorsed. The widebody franchise test is not triggered: 58% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 in every column, and no Re-engine is on the record. In 2035, if launch_if_selected is ordered again or an UltraFan is in development, the upgrade stays barred. The CEO should then put the choice to us explicitly, with the upgrade-alone row against hold (and its declared premium) set against the narrowbody option row. Bring it forward at once if a 787 or A350 Re-engine appears on the record, within the $3B cap.

The hurdle case if triggered. McCabe's stylised 21-28% IRR rests on lifecycle revenue, not margin, as she says. If an airframer selects us, bring a margin-based investment case against the mid-to-high-teens hurdle to the Audit Committee before the first full year of spend. Show the funding redeployed inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope, and confirm the dividend and the buyback cadence after 2028.

Capacity. Watson's estimate of roughly 1,100-1,900 narrowbody engines a year by 2050, if selected, is his approximation, not a grid output, but it is three to six times today's widebody OE ramp. If triggered, ring-fence Trent XWB and Trent 7000 supply and support. Bring a supplier plan (castings, forgings, gearbox) with the first-year programme review.

Next round. Watson's 'one window' point is noted: a 2035 trigger cannot serve a 2030-launched airframe, so a 2035 launch_if_selected matters only for an airframe whose EIS is at least seven years out. Read the 2035 bulletin first. If an airframer has named another engine, do not chase it; narrowbody remains an option the company does not need. Partner first on the Joint Venture, and cancel nothing that a live airframe flies.

board_review.note: The Board approves `ultrafan_nb_solo: launch_if_selected`. Safety comes first, and the package respects it. The engine would be ready in 2037, at launch plus seven and never compressed, with support in place before entry into service and no early date disclosed. The airframe goes first and we follow. The row is never below hold: 0 / +12.53 / 0 / +9.52 / +23.13 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0. It is worth +1.37 on McCabe's confirmed weights, with a worst column of 0 against an $8B bill and no premium. It carries her co-signature and Watson's concurrence, and overrides is empty. We note, and accept, that a trigger breaks our own $4B narrowbody line in the very columns where it pays most; a 2035 fold cannot repair that. The upgrade rightly waits. "We are a long-term business with very long investment cycles." And we do not want to underestimate the risks: discipline now, and the growth story if an airframer chooses us.
